shall be of the opinion that the person registered is
not lawfullyentitledto be registeredafterhearing the
proof, the committee shall direct the clerk of the
council to strike his name from the registerby insert-
ing opposite his name the words , " Stricken offby
order of the council committee .
clerk of the council." The person having the notice
served, and the person upon whom it isserved, may
each introducenot exceeding two witnesseson a side.
Within two days afteritsappointment by the council,
the committee shallhear proof of the partiesupon the
question of registration, and shall make report in
writingof the resultof its action,which reportshall
be filed with the clerk of the council within one week
afterthe appointment of the committee. If the per-
son upon whom notice is attempted to be served can
not be found , a return of that fact, sworn to and
signed by the person who endeavored to serveit,shall
be presented to the councilat itsfirstregularmeeting
or calledmeeting not lessthan fivedays afterthe date
of the notice, accompanied by motion in writing to
strike the name of the person in question from the
register; and the council, at itsnext regular meeting
afterthe filingof the motion,shallorder the council
clerk to inserton the register,opposite the name of
the person whose qualificationto registeris ques-
tioned, the following: " Doubtful ; by order of the
council . -, clerk of the council ;"
and when ,at any election, such person whose name
is marked doubtful shall offerto vote, he shall be
sworn, and his rightto vote investigatedfully.
§12. On Friday previous to the second Saturday
in June of each year,and on the day previous to any
called or special election to be held thereafter in the
cityof Mount Sterlingfor the electionof cityofficers,
the clerk of the council shall deliver to the clerks of
the election the registration books for their several
wards , togetherwith the poll-books ,which said reg-
istrationand poll-books shall be produced by said
clerks at their several wards when the polls are
opened on the day of election. At said electionthe
vote of no person shall be received unless the name
of the person offeringto vote is on the register, or
unlessthe certificateof the clerk isproduced as here-
inbefore provided .
False Registration .
§ 13. Any person who shall cause himself to be
registeredin more than one ward ,otherwise than is
provided for in sectionten of this act,or more than
once in the same ward , or who shall cause himself
to be registered,knowing that he is not twenty -one
years of age,or knowing that he is not lawfully en-
titledto registration,and any person who shall aid
or abet in the commission of any of said acts, he
shallbe deemed guiltyof a misdemeanor ,and shall
be fined not exceeding two hundred dollars, or im-
prisoned in the county jail not less than one nor
more than twelve months , or both , in the discretion
of the jury.
False Registration Books .
§ 14. Any officerof registrationor any other per-
son who shall unlawfully alterany registrationbook ,
or add any name thereto, or shall willfullysecrete,
suppress or destroy any such book , or who shall
make , or aid in making , any falseor fraudulentreg-
istrationbook , shall be deemed guilty of a felony,
and shall be confined in the penitentiarynot less
than one nor more than fiveyears,and shallforfeit
any officehe then holds, and shall be forever dis-
qualifiedfrom holding office.
§ 15. Any person who shall willfullymake any
false statement, under oath lawfully administered
under this act, shall be deemed guilty of perjury,
and confinedin the penitentiarynot lessthan one nor
more than fiveyears .
Obstructing Registration.
§ 16. Any person who ,by himself or in aid of oth-
ers, shall forciblybreak up , or attempt to break up ,
a registrationheld under thisact, or shall forcibly
prevent any person from approaching or entering a
place of registrationfor the purpose of registering,
shall be fined not less than one hundred nor more
than fivehundred dollars, or imprisoned not lessthan
six nor more than twelve months in the county jail,
or both so finedand imprisoned.
Fees .
§ 17. For his services under this act the city clerk.
shall receivethe following fees, and no other : For
copying the registrylistrequired to be kept in his
office,or to be used in supplying lostbooks ,the sum
of one cent for each voter whose name is copied ; for
his services under section eleven of this act, the sum
of ten cents for the name of each voter stricken from
the list; for receiptingto clerksof registrationand.
electionfor registrationbooks ,the sum of fivecents
foreach book receiptedfor ;he shallreceivefor serv-
ing the notice provided for in section two the sum of
twenty -fivecents for each actual service. Officers of
registrationshallreceivetwo dollarsper day foreach
day employed in attending at the place of registra-
tion,but clerksof registrationand electionshall not
be entitledto any pay ,except upon producing the re-
ceiptsof the clerkof the council,which receiptsshall
be the voucher of the officerpaying them . For his
servicesin casesarisingunder sectioneleven of this
article, each member of the committee shall receive
two dollarsper day for each day he actuallyserves.
The cityof Mount Sterlingshallpay allfeesand ex-
penses incurred under this articlefor registration,
except in contestsarisingunder sectioneleven of this
article; the person by whom , or at whose instance
the noticewas served,shall pay all costsof the pro-
ceeding in such contest, should the committee decline
to strike from the registerthe name of the person upon
whom the notice was served .
§ 18. At any time afterthe second registrationday ,
and before the next ensuing June election thereafter
for the election of city officers, the council may , in
itsdiscretion, have the registeredlistof voters, in-
cluding the name , color and local residence of each
voter,published in one of the newspapers of the city
of Mount Sterling,or the council may , in itsdiscre-
tion,have said listpublished in any other way the
councilmay deem proper.
§ 19. A copy of thisarticleshallbe printed in each
registrationbook made under itsprovisions.
ARTICLE IX .
§ 1. This actshallgo intoeffectand be in fullforce
on and afteritspassage ;and allactsand parts of acts
coming in conflictwith thisact are hereby repealed.
Approved May 23, 1890 .

laws.summary: This act incorporates the Evergreen Cemetery Company and outlines its powers and regulations. Notably, Section 13 explicitly prohibits the interment of colored persons in any lot within the cemetery, with forfeiture of the lot and improvements for any owner who attempts such an interment. The company is also empowered to prohibit such interments.

CHAPTER 1785 .
AN ACT to incorporatethe "C. T. Rice Cemetery Company ," near
Union , in Boone county .
Be it enactedby the General Assembly of the Com-
monwealth of Kentucky :
§ 1. That C. T. Rice,J. W. Conner ,James A. Huey ,
M. C. Norman and B. L. Rice , and their successors,
be, and they are hereby,createda body -corporateand
politic,under the name and style of " The C. T. Rice
Cemetery Company ;" and by that name said com -
pany shall have perpetual succession, and shall be
able and capable in law to have and use a common
seal, to sue and to be sued, plead and be impleaded ,
defend and be defended , in all courts of this Com-
monwealth and elsewhere .
§2 . They shallhave power to acquire and hold,
by purchase, gift or devise, real and personal es-
tate necessary to provide a suitable cemetery for
burialof the dead in the county of Boone and in the
vicinityof Union , not exceeding twenty-five (25)
acres of land , and of more value than two thousand
dollars($2,000), and to receivea conveyance of the
same in itscorporate name ; and when the same is so
conveyed, itshallnever be held or used forany other
purpose than that of a cemetery ; shallbe foreverfree
and exempt from all executions or other legal pro-
cess, and from any charge or assessment to or for any
public purpose inconsistentwith its use as a ceme-
tery, forwhich purpose itisforeverdedicated.
§3. The affairsof this corporation shall be man-
aged by the above-named corporators,or their repre-
sentatives, who willelectannually from theirnumber
a president, secretaryand treasurer,who shall hold
their officefor one year , and until their successors
are electedand qualified. The treasurershall exe-
cute a bond to the company , with approved security,
forthe faithfulperformance of allhisduties; and it
shallbe the duty of the treasurerto collectand to
pay out the funds of the company , and to keep a
recordthereof; but he shallpay out money only on
the orderof the president, attestedby the secretary.
The firstelectionshallbe held on the firstMonday in
January, one thousand eight hundred and ninety-
one,and annually thereafter.
§4. They shallcause to be prepared and kept an
accuratemap and survey of the grounds and lots in
saidcemetery .
§5. They shallhave power to make by -laws for the
regulationand controlof lots, and for the control,
careand management of the grounds and graves,and
the mode of ornamenting the same .
§6. They shallhave power to enterupon any of the
lotsand remove any ornaments , fixtures or shrubbery
thatmay be planted on said lotsagainst the regula-
tionsor by -laws of saidcompany .
§7 . They shall have power to sell burial lots at
eitherpublicor privatesale, and when sold it shallbe
theduty of the presidentto execute to the purchaser
a certificateof sale,giving the number of the lot or
lotsas purchased by him ,which shall vest the pur-
chaser with titleto said lot or lots, said certificateto
be attestedby the secretary; and the fullpower of
rejectingany bid for lot or lotsis reserved by the
company .
§ 8. If, from any cause,the electionis not held for
officersas herein required, then the secretaryshall

laws.summary: This section of the Kentucky Constitution, specifically Article VII concerning slaves, outlines the powers of the General Assembly regarding emancipation and the treatment of slaves. It states the Assembly cannot emancipate slaves without owner consent or compensation, can allow slave owners to emancipate slaves while protecting creditors and preventing public charge, and can prevent slaves from being brought into the state as merchandise or from foreign countries. It also mandates laws for humane treatment, clothing, provisions, and protection from injury, with provisions for selling slaves if owners fail to comply. Section 2 addresses the prosecution of slaves for felony, stating no grand jury inquest is necessary but requiring an impartial trial by a petit jury.

laws.summary: This section of the Kentucky Constitution outlines provisions related to slavery and free negroes/mulattoes. It grants the General Assembly power to regulate emancipation, prevent the immigration of free negroes and mulattoes who refuse to leave or return to the state, and punishes such individuals with felony charges and penitentiary confinement. It also addresses the prosecution of slaves for felony, stating that grand jury inquests are not necessary but petit jury trials are still a privilege. The text also includes provisions for the common school fund and the revision of the constitution.

laws.title: § 283. Colored deaf mutes—terms of admission—appropriation—officers.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 283, pp. 287–288
laws.summary: This statute mandates the admission of colored deaf and dumb pupils into the institution on the same terms as white pupils, providing equal per capita support. It also appropriates funds for a separate colored department, but crucially states that both races shall be under the same management and superintendent, with the colored department subject to the control of the board overseeing the white institution. This establishes a segregated but centrally controlled educational system for deaf and dumb individuals based on race.

laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 310, p. 293
laws.summary: This statute appropriates funds for the education of colored blind children in Kentucky, establishing a separate appropriation for their sole and exclusive use. It mandates that these funds be expended similarly to those for white blind children and that colored blind children receive equal terms of rights, benefits, and privileges. However, it also states that both races shall be under the same general management and superintendent.

laws.title: § 795. Separate coaches or compartments for white and colored passengers.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 795, p. 446
laws.summary: This statute requires railroad companies operating in Kentucky to provide separate coaches or compartments for white and colored passengers. Each compartment must be divided by a substantial wooden partition with a door and clearly marked with appropriate words indicating the race for which it is designated. The law also stipulates that there should be no discrimination in the quality, convenience, or accommodations provided for either race. Failure to comply results in a misdemeanor charge and a fine for the railroad company. The statute also includes case law interpretations regarding company liability and the constitutionality of the separate coach law.
key_provisions: § 795. Separatecoachesor compartmentsforwhiteand coloredpassengers. Any railroadcompany or corporation,person or persons,running or otherwise operating railroad cars or coaches ,by steam or otherwise ,on any railroad lineor trackwithin thisState, and allrailroadcompanies, person or persons, doing business in this State, whether upon lines of railroad owned in part or whole, or leased by them ; and allrailroadcompanies , person or persons, operating railroadlinesthat may hereafterbe built under existingcharters,or chartersthat may hereafterbe granted in this State; and allforeign corporations, companies, person or persons, or- ganized under chartersgranted,or that may be hereaftergranted,by any other State ,who may be now , or may hereafter be , engaged in running or operatingany of the railroadsof thisState,eitherin part or whole,either in their own name or that of others, are hereby required to furnish separatecoaches or cars for the travelor transportationof the white and coloredpassengers on theirrespectivelinesof railroad. Each compart- ment of a coach dividedby a good and substantialwooden partition, with a door therein,shallbe deemed a separate coach within the meaning of thisact, and each separate coach or compartment shall bear in some con- spicuousplace appropriate words in plainlettersindicatingthe race for which itissetapart. (This and secs.796-801isan act ofMay 24,1892.)

laws.title: § 799. Duties and powers of conductors of trains.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 799, p. 447
laws.summary: This statute mandates that railroad conductors assign white and colored passengers to separate cars, coaches, or compartments. Refusal to comply with the assignment allows the conductor to refuse passage or remove the passenger without liability. It also outlines penalties for conductors who fail to enforce this segregation and specifies exceptions for employees, nurses, officers in charge of prisoners, and passengers in caboose cars. The statute also addresses interference with freight and passenger transportation and coercion.
key_provisions: § 799. Dutiesandpowersofconductorsoftrains. The conductorsor managers on allrailroadsshallhave power , and are hereby required, to assign to each white or coloredpassenger hisor her respectivecar or coach or com- partment , and should any passenger refuseto occupy the car, coach, or compartment to which he or she may be assigned by the conductor or manager , said conductor or manager shallhave the right to refuse to carry such passenger on his train, and may put such passenger off of the train. And forsuch refusaland putting offthe trainneitherthe manager , conductor,nor railroadcompany shallbe liablefor damages in any court.

laws.title: § 1439. Qualification of voters.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 1439, p. 623
laws.summary: This statute outlines the qualifications for voters in Kentucky, specifying age, residency requirements, and exceptions. It lists persons convicted of treason, felony, bribery, or certain misdemeanors, those in confinement, and idiots and insane persons as ineligible to vote. It also notes that soldiers, seamen, and marines stationed in the state are not considered residents and cannot vote. Additionally, it states that payment of a poll-tax is a prerequisite for voting in municipal elections if required by the municipality's charter.
page_titles: Qualification of voters
laws.full_text:
§ 1439. Qualificationof voters. Every male citizenof the United States of
the age of twenty -one years , who has resided in the State one year , and
in the county six months , and in the precinctin which he offersto vote
sixtydays next precedingthe election,isa voterin said precinctand not
elsewhere;but the followingpersons are excepted.and shallnot have the
rightto vote: (See Con .,sec.145.)
1. Persons convictedin any court of competent jurisdictionof treason
or felony or briberyin an election, or of such high misdemeanor as the
General Assembly may declare, shall operate as an exclusion from the
right of suffrage ; but persons hereby excluded may be restored to their
civilrightsby executivepardon . (Con .,sec.150.)
2. Persons who , at the time of the election, are in confinement under
the judgment of a courtfor some penal offense.
3. Idiotsand insane persons. (See U. S. naturalizationlaw,page 32.)

laws.summary: This statute outlines the oath required for individuals to vote in Kentucky elections. It details the residency requirements, disqualifications, and the process for administering and verifying the oath. It also establishes penalties for false swearing and mandates investigation by attorneys and the grand jury to identify and prosecute illegal voters. The enforcement mechanisms and the potential for discriminatory application, particularly in the context of historical voting restrictions for Black citizens, suggest a Jim Crow era characteristic.

laws.title: § 1555. Party affiliation—provisions for registering.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 1555, pp. 661–663
laws.summary: This statute outlines the process for holding primary elections in Kentucky. It states that all legal voters have the right to participate, subject to additional political qualifications prescribed by the party committee. It also establishes a system for party affiliation registration, where individuals can declare their party preference on regular state registration books. While not explicitly mentioning race, this statute is classified as Jim Crow because the ability to impose 'additional political qualifications' by party committees, combined with the historical context of racial segregation in the South, allowed for the disenfranchisement of Black voters through discriminatory party rules and practices, effectively limiting their participation in the political process.

laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 2097, p. 857
laws.summary: This statute prohibits and declares void marriages between a white person and a negro or mulatto. It also outlines other prohibitions based on mental capacity, existing marriage, solemnization, and age. The legitimacy of children from void marriages is addressed, with specific exceptions for incestuous marriages and marriages between white persons and negroes or mulattos.
key_provisions: § 2097. Marriage- betweenwhatpersonsprohibitedandvoid. Marriage is pro- hibited and declared void : 1. With an idiot or lunatic . 2. Between a white person and a negro or mulatto . 3. Where there is a husband or wife living, from whom the person marrying has not been divorced . 4. When not solemnized or contracted in the presence of an authorized person or society. 5. When , at the time of marriage, the male is under fourteen, or the female isunder twelve years of age. (See,further,scc.2096.)

laws.full_text:
§ 2097. Marriage- betweenwhatpersonsprohibitedandvoid. Marriage is pro-
hibited and declared void :
1. With an idiot or lunatic .
2. Between a white person and a negro or mulatto .
3. Where there is a husband or wife living, from whom the person
marrying has not been divorced .
4. When not solemnized or contracted in the presence of an authorized
person or society.
5. When , at the time of marriage, the male is under fourteen, or the
female isunder twelve years of age. (See,further,scc.2096.)

laws.title: § 3222. Separate schools for colored children.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 3222, pp. 1220–1221
laws.summary: This statute outlines provisions for public schools in second-class cities, specifically addressing the education of "colored children." These colored schools are entitled to the same benefits, governed by the same rules and regulations, and subject to the same restrictions as white schools.

laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 4434, p. 1564
laws.summary: This statute outlines the requirements and election process for school district trustees. It specifies that trustees must be of good moral character and at least twenty-one years of age. Crucially, it states that for white schools, trustees must be able to read and write, while for colored schools, this is only required 'if practicable.' This differential standard for 'colored schools' indicates a potential for racial discrimination in educational administration.
key_provisions: § 4434. Number- qualification- election- term- tievote- chairman- quorum- penalty- voters. Each school districtshall be under the control of three trustees,who shallbe of good moral character, at leasttwenty-one years of age, and for white schools, able to read and write, and for colored schools, able to read and write, if practicable, one of whom shall be electedeach year forthe term of threeyears,to fillthe place of the trustee goingoutofoffice. No personholdingtheofficeoftrusteeof any private schoolshallbe eligibleto hold the officeof trusteeof any common school. The vote in electinga trusteeshallbe taken viva voce, and the election shallbe held at the schoolhouse,and ifno schoolhousebe in the district, at such convenient place as the trusteemay select, from one o'clocktill six o'clock in the afternoon on the firstSaturday of October each year , notice thereof having been posted by the trustees at three of the most public places in the districtfor ten days immediately preceding the day of election. At this election the qualifiedvoters of the districtshall be the electors;and any widow having a childbetween six and twenty years of age,and any widow or spinsterhaving a ward between the ages of six and twenty years , may also vote. Penalties are established for violations and for school officials who fail to enforce the law.

laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 4522, p. 1602
laws.summary: This statute outlines the establishment and administration of separate schools for colored children in Kentucky. It details how donations for colored schools are to be handled, the process for taking a census of colored pupils, and the election of separate trustees for white and colored schools. Crucially, it explicitly prohibits taxes levied for one racial group's schools from benefiting the other, and mandates that white children cannot attend colored schools and colored children cannot attend white schools.
key_provisions: § 4522. Donationor deviseto- by whom held. All sums arising from any donation, gift, grant or devise by any person whatsoever, wherein the intentisexpressedthatthe same isdesignedto aid in the educationof the coloredchildrenin thisCommonwealth ,or any countyor schooldistrict therein, shallbe held and used for the purposes specifiedin such dona- tion,gift,grant or devise; and the Superintendent of Public Instruction, county superintendentof common schoolsof the county, and trusteesof colored common school districts, shall receive such donations, gifts, grants or devise for the benefit of the colored schools of the State or par- ticularcounty or district,respectively,and shallhold and use the same as requested by the donor or devisor.

laws.summary: This statute outlines the establishment and administration of separate schools for colored children in Kentucky. It details how donations for colored schools are to be handled, the process for taking a census of colored pupils, and the election of separate trustees for white and colored schools. Crucially, it explicitly prohibits taxes levied for one racial group's schools from benefiting the other, and mandates that white children cannot attend colored schools and colored children cannot attend white schools.
key_provisions: § 4523. Censusof pupils- how and when taken--designationof districts. The number of coloredchildrenin each district, between the ages of six and twenty years, shallbe taken and reported at the same time and in the same manner as required by law for taking the census of white children. All coloreddistrictsshallbe designated by lettersin alphabeticalorder for each county, as DistrictA , DistrictB , and so on.

laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 45274, p. 1604
laws.summary: This statute details the renaming of the 'State Normal School for Colored Persons' to 'The Kentucky Normal and Industrial Institute for Colored Persons'. It outlines the powers and responsibilities of its board of trustees, the selection and duties of the institute's president, and the establishment of a department for agriculture and mechanics. It also specifies admission requirements for pupils, including a pledge to teach in colored common schools.
key_provisions: § 45274. Name ofschool- presidentandpowers- superintendent. That the name of the State Normal School for Colored Persons ishereby changed to that of "The Kentucky Normal and IndustrialInstitutefor Colored Persons," and its board of trustees shall be known as "The Board of Trustees of the Kentucky Normal and Industrial Institute for Colored Persons ." That the presidingofficerof the institute,who shallbe selectedby the board of trustees,shallbe styledthe "Presidentof the Institute," and shallbe the chief administrativeofficerof the institution, under the control of the board of trustees,and be ex officioa member of the board of trustees,and hold his officeindefinitely,at the willof the said board,but the superin- tendent shall have no vote in his own election or retention in office. (This section is an act of March 18 , 1902.)

laws.title: § 4762. Judgment—minor to be apprenticed—duty of clerk.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 4762, p. 1674
laws.summary: This statute outlines the legal process for identifying, trying, and punishing individuals deemed vagrants. Convicted vagrants over twenty-one years of age could be bound out to labor or sold into servitude for up to twelve months. Minors would be apprenticed until the age of twenty-one. The proceeds from the sale of a vagrant were to be used first for prosecution fees, then to pay the vagrant's debts, and any remainder was to be paid to the wife and children, or the vagrant upon completion of their term. Married men with families could be discharged if they posted bond to support their families and engage in honest work. The statute also details the rights and powers of those who purchased or took in a vagrant.

laws.title: § 2. In the prosecution of slaves for felony, no inquest by a grand jury shall be necessary, but the proceedings in such prosecutions shall be regulated by law, cx ce pt that the General Assembly shall have no power to deprive them of the privilege of an impartial trial by a petit jury.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 2, p. 77
laws.summary: Article VII of the Kentucky Constitution addresses the issue of slavery. It outlines the General Assembly's limited powers regarding emancipation, requiring owner consent or compensation. It also permits the bringing of slaves into the state by emigrants and regulates the prosecution of slaves for felony, stating that no grand jury inquest is necessary but preserving the right to a petit jury trial. It also grants the General Assembly power to compel owners to treat slaves humanely and provide for them.

laws.heading: ARTICLE X. Concerning Slaves.
laws.title: § 1.The General Assembly shall have no power to pass laws for the emancipation of Eaves, without the consent of their owners, or without paying their owners, previous to. such emancipation, a full equivalent in money, for the slaves so emancipated, and providing for their removal from the State.…
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 1, pp. 93–94
laws.summary: This section of the Kentucky Constitution outlines provisions related to slavery and the treatment of free negroes and mulattoes. It grants the General Assembly power to regulate emancipation, including requiring removal from the state, and to prevent the importation of slaves. It also makes it a felony for any free negro or mulatto to immigrate to or for any emancipated slave to remain in the state, punishable by penitentiary confinement. Additionally, it addresses the prosecution of slaves for felony, stating that grand jury inquests are not necessary but that slaves retain the right to an impartial trial by a petit jury.

27. **Pauper idiots not to be sent to asylum unless dangerous.** No order shall be made by any court or officer for sending a pauper idiot to an asylum, nor shall such idiot be received therein unless the jury by their verdict, on the inquest, shall find that he is so dangerous or uncontrollable that he can not be safely and properly kept by a committee within the county.

28. **Patients may be taken from asylum—when.** The superintendents of the several asylums shall have the right and authority to permit the family or friends of patients, whose condition of mind and health is such as, in the opinion of such superintendents, may be taken care of and treated properly outside of the asylum, to be taken from the asylum, either permanently or for such length of time as the superintendent may deem prudent.

29. **Pay patients from other states—discharge of patients—criminals—board of pay patients.** Under no circumstances shall it be permitted that, by the reception of pay patients from other States, the asylum be so crowded that any delay shall be incurred in the immediate reception of patients resident in this Commonwealth, either paying or pauper, and no person who has not been found to be insane by regular inquest shall be received into either asylum. Nor shall any patient be discharged as cured unless by the authority of the Superintendent. Any cured patient who was admitted to the asylum while in custody of the law upon a criminal charge, shall be delivered to the keeper of the penitentiary or to the jailer of the county whence he came, as the case may require. A cured pauper, before being discharged, shall have a good suit of clothes and be furnished with money enough to pay his traveling expenses back to home not exceeding twenty dollars. The Board of Control shall charge for board paying patients the sum of one hundred and fifty dollars per annum, but the Superintendent may be permitted to charge the committee or friend of paying patient an amount not exceeding $5.00 per week for special attention.

laws.title: § 310. Appropriation - annual for colored children.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 310, p. 320
laws.summary: This statute appropriates $3,000 annually for the sole and exclusive use of colored blind children, to be expended similarly to funds for white blind children. It also states that blind children of both races shall receive equal terms of rights, benefits, and privileges, but under the same general management and superintendent. The act was passed in 1909, with a prior amendment in 1906 increasing general appropriations.
key_provisions: § 310. Appropriation - annual for colored children. That the further sum of three thousand dollars be , and the same is hereby , appropriated , to be paid annually in equal quarterly installments , for the sole and exclu- sive use of the colored blind children of this Commonwealth , which money shall be expended in a similar manner and under the same limitations that the money appropriated for the use of the white blind children in said institution is now expended : Provided , however , That no portion of the sums hereby appropriated shall be paid until the building aforesaid is completed and paid for , and made ready for the use and occupation of the colored blind children of this Commonwealth , and of this fact the Auditor of Public Accounts is first duly certified in writing by the presi dent and secretary of the board of visitors of the Kentucky Institution for the Education of the Blind .

laws.heading: ARTICLE V. Railroads .
laws.title: § 799. Duties and powers of conductors of trains.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 799, p. 510
laws.summary: This statute mandates that conductors and managers of railroads must assign white and colored passengers to their respective cars, coaches, or compartments. Refusal to comply with these assignments allows the conductor to refuse passage or remove the passenger without liability for damages. Penalties are imposed on conductors who fail to enforce these provisions. The act does not apply to railroad employees, nurses, officers in charge of prisoners, or passengers in caboose cars on freight trains.
key_provisions: § 799. Dutiesandpowersofconductorsoftrains. The conductors or managers on allrailroadsshallhave power , and are hereby required, to assign to each white or coloredpassenger his or her respectivecar or coach or com- partment , and should any passenger refuse to occupy the car, coach or compartment to which he or she may be assigned by the conductor or manager , saidconductoror manager shallhave the rightto refuseto carry such passenger on his train, and may put such passenger offthe train. And forsuch refusaland puttingoffthe trainneitherthe manager , conductor,nor railroadcompany shallbe liablefordamages in any court.

laws.title: § 1399a. Slave marriages—children to inherit—children of subsequent marriage.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 1399a, p. 703
laws.summary: This statute addresses the legitimacy and inheritance rights of children born from slave marriages. It states that children born from cohabitation between enslaved individuals as husband and wife are considered lawful children and legal heirs. However, if either parent later legally marries another person and has children from that subsequent marriage, the children from the slave marriage will only inherit a proportion of the property based on the ratio of children from the slave marriage to children from the subsequent legal marriage. The act also specifies that it does not apply if the property has already been sold to innocent purchasers or divided.

laws.summary: This statute outlines the process for challenging a voter's qualifications and requires voters to take a detailed oath affirming their age, residency, and lack of felony convictions. It specifies the number of witnesses allowed in a dispute and mandates that the oath be subscribed and sworn before an election judge. The subscribed oath is to be returned to the county clerk and then to the grand jury, with penalties for failure to do so. The oath itself includes specific residency requirements and a declaration of no disqualification.

laws.summary: This statute establishes the House of Reform for young offenders under 21. It mandates separate departments for white and colored inmates. It also outlines sentencing, parole, and financial provisions for the institution.

laws.title: § 2097.Marriage—between what persons prohibited and void.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 2097, p. 987
laws.summary: This statute prohibits and declares void marriages between a white person and a negro or mulatto. It also outlines other prohibited marriages based on mental capacity, existing marital status, solemnization, and age. The statute further details the legitimacy of children from illegal or void marriages, with specific exceptions for incestuous marriages and marriages between a white person and a negro or mulatto.
key_provisions: §2097.Marriage- betweenwhatpersonsprohibitedand void. Marriage is pro- hibitedand declared void : 1.With an idiot or lunatic . 2.Betweena white person and a negro or mulatto. 3.Where there is a husband or wife living, from whom the person marryinghas not been divorced. 4.When not solemnized or contractedin the presenceof an authorized personor society. 5.When, at the time of marriage,the male isunder fourteen, or the femaleisunder twelve years of age. (See,further,sec.2096.)

§2097.Marriage- betweenwhatpersonsprohibitedand void. Marriage is pro-
hibitedand declared void :

3.Where there is a husband or wife living, from whom the person

personor society.
5.When, at the time of marriage,the male isunder fourteen, or the
femaleisunder twelve years of age. (See,further,sec.2096.)

laws.title: § 2114. Parties contracting void marriage—punishment of.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 2114, p. 990
laws.summary: This statute defines and punishes marriages between a white person and a negro or mulatto as void. It prescribes fines and imprisonment for parties entering into such marriages, and further imprisonment if they continue to cohabit after conviction.
key_provisions: § 2114. Partiescontractingvoidmarriage- punishmentof. Any party to a mar- riage within the incestuousdegreesherein prohibited, or between a white person and a negro or mulatto,shallbe finednot lessthan fivehun- dred nor more than fivethousand dollars, and if, after conviction, the partiescontinue to cohabitas man and wife,they,or eitherof them ,shall be imprisoned not less than three nor more than twelve months in the penitentiary.

instruction shall determine the amount of per capita to be paid over to the school board of such cities, by adding annually to the number of children of school age as shown by the next preceding census actually taken, such increase or addition as he may ascertain to be the annual increase of children of school age in the district upon averaging the yearly increase shown by the three actual enumerations next preceding: *Provided, however*, That the school board or superintendent of public instruction may elect to take an actual census in any of such years, in which case the return of such census shall govern. The superintendent of public instruction shall in his biennial report give statement of the estimated census for any years included in said report wherein distribution of per capita may have been made upon estimated census, as provided herein, in such manner as to show clearly the actual enumeration upon which such estimates may have been based and the manner in which the estimated census has been computed. **§ 2975. Eligibility to office of trustee.** No person shall be eligible to the office of trustee of the public schools who has not attained the age of thirty years, and who is not a housekeeper, or is not the owner of real estate in said city, or who is not a citizen of the United States, or a *bona fide* resident of the Commonwealth of Kentucky and of the legislative district of the city for which he is elected, for three years next preceding his election; or who holds or discharges any office, deputyship, or agency under the city, or any district or county, or under the State of Kentucky or any department thereof, or under the United States or any foreign government, except notaries public and militia officers of Kentucky. No person shall be eligible to this office who, at the time of his election, is directly or indirectly interested in any contract with the board, or who holds any office of trust, agency, or salary with any corporation which holds any contract with the board, or who is in any way benefited by the appropriations of the board; or whose father, son, brother, wife, daughter, or sister is employed as teacher or as professor, or in any other capacity by said board, or in any of the public schools, or who is, directly or indirectly, interested in the sale to the board of books, stationery, or other property.

**§ 2976. Member becoming disqualified—office vacated.** If, after election, any member of the board should become a candidate for nomination or for any office or agency, the holding and discharging of which would have rendered him ineligible before his election, or should he remove out of the district for which he was chosen, or should he do or incur anything which would have rendered him ineligible for election, or should any of the relatives above specified be employed by the board, his office shall become vacant and be filled as herein directed.

**§ 2977. Members privileged in debate.** Members of the board shall not be elsewhere called in question for language used in debate.

**§ 2978. Separation of white and colored children.** No white child shall become a pupil in any school for colored children, and no colored child shall become a pupil in any school for white children; but schools for white and colored children shall be kept and maintained separately.

laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 3780, p. 1598
laws.summary: This statute outlines the appointment, duties, and compensation of patrols in Kentucky counties. County courts are authorized to divide counties into districts and appoint patrols to maintain public peace and order. Patrols are tasked with visiting suspected places and places of unlawful assemblies. Compensation is based on hours of service, with a higher rate for counties with over 150,000 inhabitants. A separate section addresses the appointment of patrolmen in counties with first-class cities, with compensation paid by petitioners or employers.

laws.summary: This statute outlines the process for assessing railroad and bridge property for taxation, including the equalization of valuations by the Railroad Commission. It also details the reporting requirements for school district boundaries to railroad companies and mandates the payment of school taxes to county superintendents. laws.summary: This statute details the distribution and management of the common school fund in Kentucky. It outlines the process for estimating and apportioning funds based on pupil-child census data, the role of the Auditor and Superintendent of Public Instruction, and procedures for handling uncalled-for or unused funds. Crucially, it states that the per capita derived from interest on bonded surplus in the State Treasury shall be duly apportioned to the white and colored schools of the county respectively.

laws.summary: This statute outlines the process for dividing school districts into educational divisions and sub-districts. It explicitly mentions the inclusion of both white and colored children in these divisions and sub-districts. However, it also contains provisions that disproportionately affect Black students, such as the requirement that sub-districts must have at least fifty white children of school age to receive per capita funding for one teacher, and no more than one hundred white pupil-children for the payment of one teacher. This implies a potential underfunding or lack of resources for schools with a higher proportion of Black students.

laws.summary: This statute outlines the organization and administration of common school districts in Kentucky. It details rules for district boundaries, pupil population requirements, and the establishment of schools. Crucially, it contains a clause stating that 'nothing in this chapter shall be construed to authorize any white person to attend a common school or other institution of learning established for colored children.'

laws.title: § 4428. Teachers not having certificates can not be paid any part of the common school money.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4428, pp. 1847–1848
laws.summary: This section of the Kentucky Statutes from 1909 outlines regulations for common school districts. It includes provisions for district boundaries, the number of children required, and the location of schoolhouses. Crucially, it states that 'no white child shall be permitted to attend a common school or other institution of learning established for white children, nor shall any colored person be permitted to attend a common school or other institution of learning established for white children.' This explicitly mandates segregation in schools.

laws.title: § 4439a. Seminary property may be acquired by trustees.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4439a, p. 1854
laws.summary: This statute authorizes trustees holding legal title to county seminary property (acquired before December 18, 1865) to sell, transfer, or convey it to the trustees of white common school districts where the seminary property is located. The proceeds or property must be used for the education of white pupils, with provisions for white pupils from other districts to receive a reduction to compensate for their interest in the seminary property.

laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4464, pp. 1866–1868
laws.summary: This statute outlines the establishment and administration of graded common school districts in Kentucky. It details requirements for district boundaries, schoolhouse locations, and the process for changing district boundaries. Notably, it includes a provision (14) explicitly stating that taxes collected for white schools must be from white persons' property and taxes for colored schools must be from colored persons' property, making any apportionment between them void. This demonstrates a clear mandate for racial segregation in the funding and operation of schools.

laws.summary: This statute outlines the process for establishing graded common schools that could span two counties. It specifies that the establishment of such a school and the levying of taxes for its maintenance and construction require a vote of the 'legal white voters' within the proposed district. The statute also details requirements for petitions, approvals from county judges and superintendents, and the proximity of the schoolhouse to the district's boundary.

laws.title: § 4477. Free tuition to resident white children.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4477, p. 1873
laws.summary: This statute outlines the organization and operation of graded common school districts in Kentucky. It details the roles of trustees, president, secretary, and treasurer, as well as provisions for admitting students. Specifically, Section 4477 states that 'All white children within the common school age residing in any graded common school district shall have the right of free admission to the graded common school thereof.'
key_provisions: § 4477. Freetuitiontoresidentwhitechildren. All white children within the common school age residingin any graded common school districtshall have the right of freeadmission to the graded common school thereof.

laws.title: § 4487.Colored graded schools—establishment of.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4487, p. 1876
laws.summary: This statute explicitly mandates the segregation of schools based on race. It states that provisions for graded common school districts apply to districts organized by colored people, with the word 'colored' to be substituted for 'white' where applicable. Crucially, it prohibits white individuals from voting in colored school elections, prevents the taxation of white property for colored schools, and vice versa. It also forbids white children from attending colored schools and colored children from attending white schools.

laws.title: § 4524. Trustees—election of separate tax and schools for white and colored.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4524, p. 1892
laws.summary: This statute outlines the provisions for separate schools for colored children in Kentucky. It details how donations for colored schools are to be handled, the census of colored pupils, the election of separate trustees for white and colored schools, and prohibits inter-racial attendance in schools. It also mandates separate teachers' institutes for colored teachers and outlines penalties for non-compliance.
key_provisions: § 4524. Trustees- electionof separatetax and schoolsfor white and colored. Colored school trustees for each colored school districtshall be elected at the same time and in the same manner that white trustees are elected; but no tax shallbe leviedupon the propertyor poll, or any services requiredof any white person for the benefitof a school for coloredchil- dren;and no taxshallbe leviedupon thepropertyor poll,or any services requiredof any coloredperson for the benefitof a school for white chil- dren ; and no colored person shallbe allowed to vote for a trusteeofa whiteschool,and no whitepersonshallbe allowedtovotefora trusteeof a coloredschool. It shallnot be lawful,under any of the provisionsof thischapter,forany whitechildto attendany common schoolprovided forcoloredchildren,or forany coloredchildtoattendany common school provided for white children.

laws.title: § 4526. Penalties prescribed enforcement of.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4526, pp. 1892–1893
laws.summary: This statute mandates the separation of white and colored individuals in educational institutions. It prohibits teaching both races in the same college, school, or institution, with penalties for violations. It also makes it unlawful for individuals of one race to attend schools where the other race is received as pupils, with fines for each day of attendance. Exceptions are made for penal institutions and houses of reform. The law also allows for separate and distinct branches of private institutions in different localities, at least twenty-five miles apart, for the exclusive education of one race.

laws.summary: This statute establishes and appropriates funds for a normal school specifically for colored residents of Kentucky. It outlines admission requirements, including age, health, moral character, and a pledge to teach in colored common schools. Tuition is free for eligible colored residents. The statute also forbids sectarian teaching but promotes Christian morality. It details trustee responsibilities for school inspection and reporting, and specifies annual appropriations for teacher salaries and expenses, as well as a separate appropriation for a dormitory for female pupils. Additional appropriations for buildings and support are noted from earlier acts.

laws.summary: This statute establishes two State Normal School districts, Eastern and Western Kentucky, with the Eastern located in Richmond and the Western in Bowling Green. It outlines the object of these schools as providing training for teachers to make common schools efficient. Notably, it states that diplomas from the normal department will entitle teachers to teach in any of the 'colored common schools' of the state. The districts are to be divided based on white population.

laws.summary: This statute outlines the process for appointing students to state normal schools. It specifies that each county is entitled to appoint one white pupil for every five hundred white schoolchildren, based on the school census. The county superintendent is responsible for examining applicants and selecting those with the highest qualifications and good character. The statute also details the duration of appointments and how vacancies are to be filled. A key provision requires appointed pupils to sign a declaration to teach in public schools for a specified period, or pay fees.

laws.summary: This statute details the allocation of interest from a perpetual bond of the Commonwealth of Kentucky to two educational institutions: the Agricultural and Mechanical College of Kentucky and the State Normal School for Colored Persons of Kentucky. The total annual interest of $4,950 is divided, with $627.75 allocated to the State Normal School for Colored Persons and $4,322.25 to the Agricultural and Mechanical College. This section is derived from an act of May 21, 1897, which also included initial appropriations to these institutions.

laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4636a, pp. 1931–1934
laws.summary: This statute amends the law regarding student appointments to the State University (Agricultural and Mechanical College). It specifies that each county is entitled to appoint one white pupil for every three thousand white schoolchildren, and one for each fraction thereof over fifteen hundred, based on the last official census. Each county is guaranteed at least one annual appointment. The statute also outlines the selection process through competitive examinations open to individuals between fourteen and twenty-four years old, with preference given to those who have passed through public schools, possess energy and industry, and have limited means. The selection is made by county superintendents. Additionally, it mentions free tuition for students of the ministry at the university's discretion.

**Sec. 4425. Certificates to teachers — subjects upon which examined — time of examination — questions by State board of examiners — examination of teachers — how conducted.** County certificates shall be granted by the county board of examiners to persons not under eighteen years of age, upon written examinations upon the science and art of teaching, and upon the subjects embraced in the common school course, including, in connection with physiology and hygiene, the effects of alcoholic drinks and narcotics upon the human system, held in each county of the State, for white teachers, upon the third Friday and Saturday in May, June, July, and August, of each year, and for colored teachers upon the fourth Friday and Saturday of the same months, and no examinations shall be held at any other time whatever. No certificate shall be issued upon the days of examination, nor shall any answers be passed upon in the presence of any applicant. The State board of examiners shall carefully prepare four series of questions for white teachers, and an equal number for colored teachers, all of the same grade; shall inclose in a separate envelope such number of questions of each given series as the county superintendent shall make requisition for at least twenty days before the examination, with the name of the subject plainly written or printed across the seal thereof; shall inclose the several envelopes in a package, which they shall seal and forward by registered mail or by express to each county superintendent at least two weeks before the examination, designating the month for which the same shall be used. The county superintendent shall carefully preserve the said package of questions under seal until the hour of examination; and the seal of the said package shall then be examined by the other examiners and the applicants for certificates, and the package shall be opened in their presence. Immediately after examining the package of questions each of the county examiners shall, under his oath as examiner, upon blanks furnished for that purpose by the superintendent of public instruction, give a separate certificate, with signature attested by two reliable witnesses, that he had personally inspected the said package, and whether he had found the same intact, as provided herein, and forward the certificate to the superintendent of public instruction on the same day. The examiners shall allot a reasonable time for the examination upon each subject, taking the subjects in the order named in the section specifying the subjects embraced in the common school course, and shall collect the answers of all the applicants when the time allotted has expired, and, after the first subject is presented to the applicant, the said examiners shall not present any other subject, or open the envelope thereof, until they collect the answers of all applicants to all questions previously presented. The said examiners shall not examine any applicant until they are fully satisfied that said applicant possesses an unexceptional moral character, and is of the age herein prescribed; and in no event shall a certificate be granted to any person who indulges in drunkenness, profanity, gambling or licentiousness, or who, within the belief of the examiners, has had improper access to the examination questions. laws.title: Sec. 1. Parents, guardians, etc., to send children to school—age of children—exceptions. That every parent, guardian or other person in the State of Kentucky having the control of any child or children between the ages of seven and fourteen years, shall be required to send such child or children…
laws.citation: Annoted Supplement to The Kentucky Statutes Edition 1894, 1899, § 1, p. 121
laws.summary: This act mandates that parents or guardians send children between the ages of seven and fourteen to school for at least eight consecutive weeks annually. It outlines exceptions, including home schooling, physical or mental incapacity, poverty preventing proper clothing, prior acquisition of required branches, or the absence of a school within two miles for either white or colored children.
key_provisions: Sec. 1. **Parents, guardians, etc., to send children to school — age of children — exceptions.** That every parent, guardian or other person in the State of Kentucky having the control of any child or children between the ages of seven and fourteen years, shall be required to send such child or children, annually, at least eight weeks of which attendance shall be consecutive, to some public or private day or night school for children. Provided, however, that this act shall not apply in any case where the child has been or is being taught at home in such branches as are taught in public schools for a like period of time, and subject to the same examinations as other pupils of the district or city in which the child resides, or whose physical or mental condition renders his or her attendance impracticable, or who is excused by the trustees of the public school district, or the board of education of the city in which the parent, guardian or person having control resides, upon its being shown to their satisfaction that the parent, guardian or person having control was not able, by reason of poverty, to clothe such child properly, or that he or she has already acquired the ordinary branches required by law, or that there is no white school, in the case of white children, or colored school, in the case of colored children, taught within two miles by the nearest traveled road.

Whenever the number of patients sent to either asylum is greater than can be properly accommodated and cared for in that institution, and there is at the time capacity for the reception and care of the patient at either…
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Second Edition, 1899, § 250, p. 266
laws.summary: This statute outlines the procedures for managing patients in insane asylums in Kentucky. It covers the costs of returning patients, reporting asylum capacity to the Governor for patient transfers, receiving patients when other asylums are full, and specifies that white and colored patients shall not be kept in the same buildings. It also addresses the admission of pauper idiots, the release of patients to friends or family, and the reception of pay patients from other states, ensuring that residents of Kentucky are prioritized. Patients charged with crimes are also mentioned in relation to their discharge.
key_provisions: § 250. **Asylum unable to accommodate—patients may be received in another asylum.** Whenever the number of patients sent to either asylum is greater than can be properly accommodated and cared for in that institution, and there is at the time capacity for the reception and care of the patient at either of the other asylums, it shall be the duty of the commissioners and superintendent of such other to receive as many of those rejected at the former, for want of room, as can be properly accommodated. When, upon application to the proper asylum, the patient is rejected for want of room, immediate application shall be made to another. The Governor is empowered and directed to take care that each of the asylums is kept full to its utmost capacity, of such patients as are receivable by it, as long as any such patients in the State are unprovided for, and that each receives its due proportion of the patients in excess of the ordinary capacity of the asylum; and white and colored patients shall not be kept in the same buildings.

laws.title: § 282. Colored deaf mutes—institution for.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Second Edition, 1899, § 282, p. 273
laws.summary: This statute establishes a separate institution for the education of colored deaf mutes in Danville, Kentucky. It mandates that this institution be under the control of the same board of commissioners as the institution for white deaf mutes, but explicitly states that the two races shall be 'forever kept entirely separate and distinct from each other.' It also outlines terms of admission, per capita support, and an appropriation for the colored deaf mutes' institution, ensuring they receive the same terms and per capita support as white pupils.
key_provisions: § 282. Colored deaf mutes—institution for. That an institution for the education of the colored deaf mutes be established at Danville, Ky., which shall be under the general control and management of the same board of commissioners as now have charge of the institution for the white deaf mutes. But the two races shall be forever kept entirely separate and distinct from each other.

laws.title: § 796. No discrimination in coaches or compartments.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Second Edition, 1899, § 796, p. 430
laws.summary: This statute mandates that railroad companies operating in Kentucky must provide separate coaches or cars for white and colored passengers. It specifies that a compartment divided by a partition with a door counts as a separate coach. The statute also states that there should be no discrimination in the quality, convenience, or accommodations between the separate facilities. Conductors are empowered to assign passengers to their designated cars and to remove those who refuse to comply. Penalties are outlined for both railroad companies and conductors who fail to adhere to these provisions. The statute explicitly mentions "white and colored passengers."

laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Second Edition, 1899, § 1490, pp. 624–625
laws.summary: This statute outlines the process for voter registration in cities and towns in Kentucky. It details the duties of the county clerk in preparing registration books, the requirements for registration officers to attend voting places, and the information to be recorded in the registration book, including the voter's name, residence, and whether they are white or colored. It also specifies that voters must appear in person to register and may be sworn and interrogated if not personally known to an officer or if challenged by a bystander.

laws.summary: This statute outlines the administration of Houses of Reform, focusing on inmate reformation and self-support through vocational training. It includes provisions for the transfer of minor convicts from penitentiaries to these houses and mandates the separation of white and colored inmates into distinct departments. It also details appropriations for the maintenance of these institutions.

**4. Board of trustees a corporation—powers.** The trustees shall be a corporation, by the name of "The Board of Trustees of the Houses of Reform," for the purpose of taking and holding unto themselves and their successors, in trust for the State, any grant or devise of land, and any donation or bequest of money or other personal property, made for the use of said institutions, and for the purpose of preserving and investing the proceeds thereof in good securities, with all powers incident to, and necessary to, the exercise of the powers aforesaid, and to carry out and fulfill the purposes of this act. The funds, property and estate that may be granted to, or held by, such corporation for the uses hereinbefore expressed shall, with the income thereof, be exempted from taxation.

**5. Buildings to be erected—provisions concerning.** The said board, having selected sites as aforesaid for the said institutions, shall immediately deposit with the Secretary of the State a certificate of their determination, together with all conveyances of land granted and securities for moneys or material donated. They shall also prepare, or cause to be prepared, and adopt plans for the grounds, buildings and fixtures necessary for said institutions, of such form, style, dimension and finish as, when completed, shall come within the cost and limit of the sum hereinbefore appropriated. The trustees shall, in the preparation and adoption of plans for the necessary buildings, keep in view, if practicable, the possible future enlargement and improvement of said buildings, and so arrange the plans that such enlargement can be made without materially affecting their symmetry or usefulness.

**6. Contracts for buildings—concerning.** Said board of trustees shall advertise for proposals for the erection and construction, furnishing, et cetera, of said buildings, and fix a time within which said proposals will be received, and upon the expiration of such time, they may, in their discretion, and with the approval of the Governor, make contracts with the lowest responsible bidder, taking into consideration the price, time of performance and responsibility of the contractors. Said contract or contracts, when made and properly evidenced, shall be deposited in the office of the Secretary of State.

**7. Plan of buildings—regulations for inmates.** In the construction of the buildings herein provided for, and in the arrangement of the grounds, all cells, bars and grates shall, as far as practicable, be omitted, and what is known as the "Cottage Family Plan" shall be adopted, as it commends itself by accomplished facts as the most intelligent, economical and successful system in use. Each of these family houses shall be occupied by from eighteen to twenty-five girls or boys, with their matron, teacher and housekeeper. The inmates of each cottage shall be as nearly as is possible of the same character, as regards innocence or culpability, and each of said cottages, in their general arrangement and discipline, resemble, as nearly as is possible or practicable, a well ordered and regulated home.

**8. Rules for government of inmates.** The object of these institutions shall be, not merely a place of detention, but the reformation of those who, by reason of vicious conduct or moral depravity, have rendered themselves

laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Second Edition, 1899, § 3222, p. 1174
laws.summary: This statute outlines the powers and duties of a municipal board of education in Kentucky, including the admission of pupils from beyond city limits, the appointment and dismissal of employees, the establishment of a board of examiners, and crucially, the provision and maintenance of separate schools for colored children. These separate schools are to be supported and governed in a similar manner to schools for white children, receiving the same benefits and being subject to the same rules and restrictions.
key_provisions: § 3222. **Separate schools for colored children.** The said board of education shall provide, maintain and support separate schools wherein all colored children, who are *bona fide* residents of said city, between the ages of six and twenty years, may be taught in like manner as herein provided for white children; said colored schools shall be entitled to the same benefits, be governed by the same rules and regulations, and be subject to the same restrictions as the schools herein provided for the white children.

laws.heading: ARTICLE V. CountySuperintendent.
laws.title: § 4401. Election and term of office—exception in counties having cities of first class.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Second Edition, 1899, § 4401, p. 1495
laws.summary: This statute outlines the election process for county superintendents and establishes residency requirements. Notably, in counties with cities of the first or second class that maintain separate school systems, the county superintendent must reside outside of these cities and be elected only by voters residing outside these cities. This provision implicitly creates a segregated electoral and administrative structure for education.
page_titles: County Superintendent Election and Residency Requirements
laws.full_text: § 4401. Election and term of office—exception in counties having cities of first class. The county superintendent shall be elected by the qualified voters of each county at the November election in one thousand eight hundred and ninety-three, shall enter upon the discharge of the duties of his office on the second Monday in August, one thousand eight hundred and ninety-four, and continue in office until the first Monday in January, one thousand eight hundred and ninety eight, and until the election and qualification of his successor. And in one thousand eight hundred and ninety-seven, and every four years thereafter, there shall be, in each county an election of a county superintendent, who shall hold his office four years from the first Monday in January following his election, or until the election and qualification of his successor. The county school superintendent shall be elected, and the vote canvassed and the result certified by the same officers, and in the same manner as in the election of other county officers; and within ten days after the election the clerk of the county court shall forward a copy of the certificate of election to the Superintendent of Public Instruction. All county superintendents in office at the time of the November election one thousand eight hundred and ninety-three shall continue in office until the second Monday in August, one thousand eight hundred and ninety-four, or until their successors are elected and qualified. In cases of controverted right to the office of county superintendent, the Superintendent of Public Instruction shall have power to recognize a superintendent from among the contestants until the case has been settled: *Provided*, That in counties containing cities of the first or second class maintaining a system of public schools separate and distinct from the common schools of the county, the county superintendent shall reside in the portion of the county outside of such city, or cities, and be elected by the qualified voters of said county residing outside of such city or cities. (Section as amended by act of May 13, 1897.)

It mandates that the word 'colored' be substituted for 'white' where it previously appeared in the law. key_provisions: § 4487. **Colored graded schools—establishment of.** The provisions of this law shall apply to such graded common school districts as may be applied for and organized by the colored people of this Commonwealth, and such districts and graded schools may be organized by them, in all cases, the same as the white districts herein provided for are organized. In that case the word "colored" is to be substituted for the word "white" whenever it has occurred heretofore in this law. laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Second Edition, 1899, § 4530, p. 1548
laws.summary: This statute establishes and outlines the operation of a normal school specifically for colored persons in Kentucky. It details the powers of the trustees regarding curriculum, instructors, and admission criteria, including a pledge for graduates to teach in colored common schools. Tuition is free for eligible colored residents of Kentucky. The statute also specifies funding and reporting requirements for the school.
key_provisions: § 4530. **Pupils—terms of admission of.** Any pupil to gain admission to the privileges of instruction in said normal school shall be at least sixteen years of age, possess good health, satisfactory evidence of good moral character, and sign a written pledge, to be filed with the principal, that said applicant will, as far as practicable, teach in the colored common schools of Kentucky a period equal to twice the time spent as a pupil in said normal school, together with such other conditions as the board may, from time to time, impose. But no such pledge shall be required of pupils who matriculate in the departments of agriculture or mechanics.

laws.summary: This section of the Kentucky Constitution, as presented in the 1922 statutes, outlines the limits on indebtedness for various municipalities, including cities and counties. Crucially, it references a specific case (Moss v. City of Mayfield) where a proposition to incur indebtedness for school buildings for 'colored schools' was rightly submitted to 'colored voters.' This implies a system of separate educational facilities based on race, a hallmark of Jim Crow legislation, even though the primary focus of the statute is on fiscal limitations.

§ 157a . An election by the voters of a county
on the question whether the fiscalcourt shall issue
county bonds for road and bridge purposes , may
be held on a day other than the regular election
CONSTITUTION OF THE STATE OF KENTUCKY LXXXIII
day. Albright v. Ballard, Judge , 164 Ky . 747,
176 S. W. 185 .
So far as Ky . Stats., § 4308 purports to au-
thorizea levy exceeding twenty cents (20 cents)
on the one hundred dollars ($ 100.00) it is uncon-
stitutional. Mitchellv.Knox Co. FiscalCourt,165
Ky . 543 , 177 S. W. 279.
In an electionheld under Ky . Stats., § 4307,
it is not necessary that the petition for the elec-
tion should lie over from one term of the county
court to another before the court can call the
election. Finley v . Rose , County Judge , 165 Ky .
408 , 177 S. W. 433 .
This section annuls § 177 in so far as it forbids
the commonwealth to lend its credit for the con-
struction of highways . Mitchell v .Knox Co. Fiscal
Court , 165 Ky . 543 , 177 S. W. 279 .
The provision in Ky . Stats., $ 4307 , in which
the words " and bridges " is added after the word
" roads," in submission of the question of a bond
issue, is to make more specific the power con-
ferred by the constitution . Denton v . Pulaski
County , 170 Ky . 33, 185 S. W. 481 .
Under this section and Ky . Stats., $ 4307 , the
fiscal court has no discretion as to the issuance
and sale of bonds for the construction of public
roads and bridges, voted by the county , and
mandamus will lie to compel it to issue such bonds .
Houston v . Boltz, 169 Ky . 640 , 185 S. W. 76 .
Under this section an indebtedness for a pub-
lieroad may be authorizedby a majority of the
votersparticipatingin the election. Houston v .
Boltz, 169 Ky . 640 , 185 S. W. 76.
Under thissectionand Ky . Stats., $ 4748b, sub-
sec.9, it is not competent in a proceeding to pur-
chaseturnpikes, to proceed partlyunder the stat-
ute relatingto the buying of privately owned
turnpikes, and partly under the constitution re-
lating to the constructionof public roads and
bridgesby the county. Houston v.Boltz, 169 Ky .
640, 185 S. W. 76 .
This section is complete in itself, and must
be treated as independent of other sections of
the Constitution. Bird v. Asher, 170 Ky . 726, 186
S. W. 663 .
Under this section and $ 157 the fiscal court
may , in itsdiscretion, appropriatesuch portion
of the state aid road fund and of the general
road tax levied under $ 157 as it deems proper
for the payment of such indebtedness . Bird v .
Asher, 170 Ky . 726, 186 S. W. 663.
Under this section and § 157 , and Ky . Stats.,
4307 , the county is prohibited from incurring
an indebtedness for road purposes which cannot
be paid by the 20 -cent tax levy within the time
in which such indebtedness will mature . Bird v .
Asher , 170 Ky . 726, 186 S. W. 663 .
Ky . Stats ., § 4308, authorizing a levy of thirty
eents (30 cents) on the one hundred dollars
($100.00), is invalid as to the excess over the
constitutionallimit. Clearyv. Pieper, 169Ky.434 , 184 S. W. 4 .
Under this section highway bonds may be issued
and ratifiedby a majority of those voting at the
election. Armstrong v . Fiscal Court of Carter
County , 169 Ky . 433 , 184 S. W. 4 .
Under this sectiona county indebtednessfor
road purposes may be created by a majority vote
of those participatingin the election. Cleary v .
Pieper, 169 Ky . 434, 184 S. W. 4.
Under $ 157a and Ky . Stats., $ 4307, an elec-
tion specially called to determine whether road
and bridge bonds shall be issued, was properly
held on same day with the general November
election. Houston v.Boltz,169 Ky .640, 185 S. W.
76 .
Under this section and § 157, and Ky . Stats.,
$ 4307 , it was held that an election at which an
issue of county road bonds was authorized was
not invalid because two- thirds of all the legal
voters of the county did not vote to issue the
bonds . Bowman v . Fayette County , 168 Ky . 524 ,
182 S. W. 633 .
Under this section and § 157 , the fiscal court
may levy a tax of fiftycents (50 cents) on each
one hundred dollars ($100.00) of taxable prop-
erty, for purposes other than school, and an ad-
ditional tax not exceeding twenty cents (20
cents) on each one hundred dollars ($ 100.00) for
the payment of interest on road bonds and for
sinking fund for their payment . Mitchell v . Knox
Co. Fiscal Court, 165 Ky . 543, 177 S. W. 279.
Section 157 does not apply to the incurring of
indebtedness for road purposes under $ 157a . Gat-
ton v. Fiscal Court of Daviess County, 169 Ky .
426 , 184 S. W. 1 .
Under this section and §§ 157 , 158 , an amend-
ment to the constitution or statute should not be
considered as a part of the original, but as hav-
ing the effectof a codicilto a will. Gatton v . Fis-
cal Court of Daviess County , 169 Ky . 426 , 184
S. W. 1 .
Section 177 of the constitution is changed by
§157a , adopted in 1909 , providing that the credit
of the commonwealth may be pledged for public
road purposes, and Ky . Stats., § 4356x, subsec.
4 , levying a state road tax is constitutional. Mit-
chell v . Knox County Fiscal Court , 165 Ky . 543 ,
177 S. W. 279 .
The good roads amendment " (Const ., § 157a )
was held to have been duly proclaimed and pub-
lishedby publicationin two daily papers by the
legislature. Denton v.PulaskiCounty, 170 Ky .33,
185 S. W. 481 .
Under this article of the constitution and Ky .
Stats., $4307, road bonds may be submittedto
the voters at an electionheld on a day other than
a regular electionday . Albright v. Ballard, 164
Ky . 747, 176 S. W. 185 .
In determiningthe amount of a city'sindebted-
ness as compared with its annual income , an in-
debtedness contracted by a vote of the people

the sum necessary to pay annual running expenses .

for a sinking fund. Ballard v. Shelbyville, 180

Bonds of a city for the cost of improvements

school buildings for the colored schools, to be

Contractsfor localimprovements in a city, the

city. A bond issueto pay the city'sproportionate

rules. Castle v . City of Louisa , 187 Ky . 397, 219
