laws.summary: This section of the Kentucky Constitution, as interpreted in 1922, addresses the incurring of municipal indebtedness for public schools. Specifically, it details how indebtedness for school buildings for colored schools should be submitted to colored voters and how the taxable property of colored persons should be considered in determining the debt limit. It also mentions separate free graded public school districts for white and colored children occupying the same territory.

laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 187, p. 124
laws.summary: This section of the Kentucky Constitution mandates that in the distribution of school funds, no distinction shall be made on account of race or color, and that separate schools for white and colored children shall be maintained. It also notes that the distribution of the school fund is subject to legal interpretation and that 'colored children' has a defined meaning in legal contexts. The text also touches upon the financing of separate school districts for white and colored children.

laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 282, p. 326
laws.summary: This statute establishes a separate institution for the education of colored deaf mutes at Danville, Kentucky. It mandates that this institution be under the control of the same board of commissioners as the institution for white deaf mutes, but explicitly states that the two races shall be forever kept entirely separate and distinct from each other.

But the two races shallbe forever kept entirelyseparateand distinctfrom each other .

laws.summary: These sections of the 1922 Kentucky Statutes address appropriations and per capita allowances for the Kentucky School for the Deaf. Notably, § 298d-2 and § 298d-3 explicitly state that the per capita allowance made to white deaf pupils shall also apply to colored deaf pupils. This indicates a system where separate provisions were made for different racial groups, a hallmark of Jim Crow legislation, even if the intention was to provide equal per capita amounts. The statutes also cover compulsory education for deaf children and appropriations for teachers' salaries.

laws.title: § 311. Colored children; provision for education.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 311, p. 334
laws.summary: This statute mandates that blind children, when buildings are erected, are entitled to equal rights, benefits, and privileges as white blind children. However, it specifies that blind children of both races shall be under the same general management and superintendent of the Kentucky Institution for the Education of the Blind. It also mentions a separate appropriation for colored blind children.
key_provisions: §311. Colored children; provision for education . That the blind children afore- said, when such buildings shall have been erected,shall be entitled to receive on equal terms their due proportion, according to numbers,of rights, benefits, and privileges secured to the white blind children of this commonwealth by the act establishingthe Kentucky institutionfor the education of theblind, and allsubsequent enactments in relationthereto: Provided , however , That the blind children of both races shall be under the same general management and under one and the same superintendent, who , with all other officers of said institu- tion, shall be elected by , and subject in allrespectsto the supervisionand controlof the board of trustees of said institution as heretoforeprovided by law.

laws.title: § 331b-2. Warrant for $5,000 in June, 1902.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 331b-2, pp. 357–358
laws.summary: This statute regulates the importation of dependent children into Kentucky for placement in family homes. It requires individuals or institutions to provide a bond to the county judge, ensuring that imported children are not incorrigible, of unsound mind or body, or suffering from contagious/incurable diseases. The statute mandates reporting of placed children, removal of those who become public charges or are convicted of crimes, and placement under written contracts for proper care, education, and training. It also requires annual visits and reports to the Kentucky Children's Home Society. Crucially, the statute explicitly states that appropriations are for the care, support, maintenance, and supervision of 'homeless and destitute white children of this commonwealth'.

laws.title: § 795. Separate coaches or compartments for white and colored passengers.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 795, pp. 596–597
laws.summary: This statute mandates that railroad companies operating in Kentucky must provide separate coaches or compartments for white and colored passengers. It applies to all railroad lines within the state and to companies doing business in the state, whether on owned or leased lines, including those built under existing or future charters.
key_provisions: § 795. Separate coaches or compartments for white and colored passengers.- Any railroad company or corporation ,person or persons, running or otherwise operating railroad cars or coaches ,by steam or other- wise, on any railroadline or track within thisstate, and all railroadcompanies , per- son or persons , doing business in this state, whether upon lines of railroad owned in railroadcompanies ,person or persons,oper- ating railroad lines that may hereafter be built under existing charters , or charters that may hereafterbe granted in thisstate; § 796 394CORPORATIONS ; PRIVATE and all foreign corporations, companies , person or persons,organized under charters granted, or that may be hereaftergranted, by any other state, who may be now , or may herafter be, engaged in running or operating any of the railroadsof thisstate, eitherin part or whole, eitherin their own name or that of others, are hereby required to furnish separate coaches or cars for the travel or transportation of the white and colored passengers on their respectivelinesof railroad. Each compart- ment of a coach divided by a good and sub- stantial wooden partition, with a door therein, shall be deemed a separate coach within the meaning of this act, and each separate coach or compartment shall bearin some conspicuous place appropriate words in plain lettersindicatingthe race for which itisset apart. laws.summary: This statute requires all railroad companies, both domestic and foreign, operating in Kentucky to provide separate coaches or cars for white and colored passengers. It specifies that a compartment divided by a partition with a door counts as a separate coach and mandates that these compartments be clearly labeled with the race for which they are designated. The statute also includes provisions for equal accommodations and penalties for non-compliance, as well as clarifying the liabilities of companies and conductors.

laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 799, p. 700
laws.summary: This statute mandates that conductors and managers of railroads assign white and colored passengers to their respective cars, coaches, or compartments. It grants conductors the right to refuse passage or remove passengers who do not comply with these assignments, and exempts the railroad company, conductor, or manager from liability for damages in such cases. It also outlines penalties for conductors who fail to enforce these provisions.
key_provisions: §799 . Duties and powers of conductors of trains . laws.summary: This statute outlines the procedures for voter registration in Kentucky cities of the first, second, third, and fourth classes. It details the appointment of registration officers, the process for challenging a person's right to register, the requirement for personal appearance and potential swearing-in, and the recording of voter information including race ('white or colored'). The statute mandates that a person must be registered to vote and specifies the information to be included in the registration book, such as name, residence, precinct, ward, and color.

Said listof voters shallbe in alphabeticalorder [the number of the precinct and the number of the ward , if the city be warded off] the name of the streetor alley,and number of house , lodging or tenement in which he lives, and whether he be white or colored; and if said house , lodging or tenement be not num- bered , the location thereof shall be de- scribed in the registration book as accur- ately as is practicable, giving the street , and between what streets. It was error to instruct the jury to the effect
that the accused might act in self-defense if he
was in great danger of death or bodily harm ;
the instruction should have stated that he had
a right to act if it appeared to him in the exercise
of a reasonable judgment that he was in danger
of death or great bodily harm . Hoskins v . Com .,
145 Ky . 580 , 140 S. W. 1040 .
Certain instructions in a murder case as to
mental unsoundness were held proper. Banks v.
Com ., 145 Ky . 800 , 141 S. W. 380.
On the trial of an indictment for murder it
was proper to allow a non -expert witness who was
well acquainted with the defendant to express
an opinion as to whether the defendant had a
mind sufficientto know right from wrong . Banks
v . Com ., 145 Ky . 800, 141 S. W. 380 .
Certain instructions on self-defense were ap-
proved . Carnes v. Com ., 146 Ky . 425 , 142 S. W.
723 .
An instruction on a trial of indictment for
murder which omitted the element of malice afore-
thought was erroneous . Watkins v . Com ., 146 Ky .
449 , 142 S. W. 1035 .
An instruction as to self-defense which told
the jury that the defendant had the right to use
only such means as were necessary or as appeared
to him reasonably necessary to ward off the real
or apparent danger to himself was approved by
the court of appeals. Salisbury v . Com ., 146 Ky .
730 , 143 S. W. 371 .
On an indictment for murder the defendant was
found guilty of voluntary manslaughter . An in-
struction , which did not contain the words " or in
sudden affray," was held not to have been pre-
judicialto defendant. Peace v. Com ., 146 Ky . 754,
143 S. W. 399 .

It is not error to omit the word " feloniously"
from an instruction on a trial for murder . Carson
v . Com ., 149 Ky . 294 , 149 S. W. 30.
A certain indictment for wilful murder was
sufficient. Greer v. Com ., 164 Ky . 396 , 175 S. W.
665 .

laws.title: § 2114. Parties contracting void marriage; punishment of.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 2114, p. 1219
laws.summary: This statute prohibits marriages between a white person and a negro or mulatto, classifying such marriages as void. It imposes a fine of not less than $500 nor more than $5,000 on parties contracting such a marriage. If, after conviction, the parties continue to cohabit as man and wife, they face imprisonment of not less than three nor more than twelve months in the penitentiary.
key_provisions: § 2114. Parties contracting void mar- riage; punishment of.- Any . party to a marriage within the incestuous degrees hereinprohibited,or between a white per- son and a negro or mulatto, shall be fined not lessthan fivehundred dollars ($500.00) nor more than fivethousand dollars($5,- 000.00),and if,afterconviction,the parties continueto cohabitas man and wife,they, or eitherof them , shallbe imprisoned not less than three nor more than twelve months inthepenitentiary.

laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 2062c, pp. 1309–1310
laws.summary: This statute appropriates $5,000 annually for the benefit of the Red Cross Association (colored) for the purpose of equipping a hospital to care for indigent sick of the colored race. The hospital is to be supervised and cared for by their own people, and will include a nurses' training school for girls of the colored race. It also mandates at least five beds for sick and invalid colored children and those from various colored institutions. Funds are restricted to equipment, maintenance, nurses, matron, food, medicines, and physicians' services, explicitly excluding officers' salaries. A bond of $10,000 is required, and annual verified statements of expenditures are mandated.

laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 3588, pp. 2026–2027
laws.summary: This statute mandates that the board of education provide and maintain suitable buildings, teachers, and employees for all children between six and eighteen years of age. Crucially, it requires separate buildings for the education of white and colored pupils, explicitly stating that no white child shall attend a colored school, nor shall any colored child be allowed to attend a white school.
key_provisions: § 3588. Board of education may maintain man- damus proceedings against city council to compel it to pay money to which board is entitled. City v . Board of Education , 21 R. 731 ; 52 S. W. 969 . School elections . Members of the board of education must be elected by a viva voce vote , and allpersons who may vote under the general school law (§4434 ) are entitled to vote at the election. Moss v . Riley, 19 R. 993 ; 43 S. W. 421 ; 102 Ky . 1 ; but in City v . Board of Education , 21 R. 731 ; 52 S. W. 969 ; it is held that although board of education was elected by secret ballot the election was valid, as there was no contest and no complaint about itsfairness, and see Elliott v . Burke , 113 Ky . 479 ; 24 R. 292 ; 68 S. W. 445, holding that an election of the board of education by secret ballot is void . See , further, as to school elections. Trustees v . Stone , 142 Ky . 715 ; 135 S. W. 307 . laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 3588a, p. 2027
laws.summary: This statute mandates that the board of education provide and maintain suitable buildings, teachers, and employees for all children between six and eighteen years of age. Crucially, it requires separate buildings for the education of white and colored pupils, explicitly stating that no white child shall attend a colored school, nor shall any colored child be allowed to attend a white school.
key_provisions: § 3588a. The territoryof a cityof the fourth class was organized into two separate free graded publicschooldistricts,one forwhitechildrenand one for colored children. Each of these districts was a separatemunicipality, and so was the city; each of these three municipalitiesoccupied the same territory. A proposition to incur indebtedness for schoolbuildingsfor the coloreddistrictto be paid by taxation on property of colored citizens was rightlysubmitted under constitution§ 157, to colored voters . The indebtedness under constitu- tion, § 158, could not exceed two per cent (2 % ) of the taxablepropertyof coloredpersonsand the proportionof corporateproperty that the number of colored children bore to the whole number of children. Mossv.CityofMayfield,186Ky.330;216 S. W. 842 . Limitation under the five-year statute runs in favor of trusteesof a white school against the trusteesof a coloredschoolfor taxes paid to the trusteesof the white schoolby mistake. It begins to run at the time of payment . There is no lia- bilityfor intereston the claim until demand is made . Trustees Graded Free Colored, etc. v. Trus- tees Graded Free White , etc., 181 Ky . 810; 205 S. W. 904 . Money raisedby a tax from property of cor- porations in a fourth class city for free white common graded schools, must be apportioned be- tween the white and the colored graded schools. TrusteesGradedFreeColoredCommon Schoolsof Mayfieldv.TrusteesGradedFreeWhiteCommon Schools of Mayfield, 180 Ky . 574; 203 S. W. 520.

laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 4098, p. 2256
laws.summary: This statute outlines the apportionment of school taxes collected from railroad and bridge companies. It mandates that taxes levied in any common school district shall be paid to the county superintendent for the benefit of that district. Crucially, it specifies that these funds, when collected, shall be apportioned and distributed between white and colored common school districts located within the same boundaries, based on the ratio of white to colored children of pupilage residing in the district. The statute explicitly states that its provisions shall not be construed to apply to any colored school district, but then proceeds to detail the racial apportionment of funds collected from railroad and bridge companies.

laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 4420a-3, p. 2414
laws.summary: This statute outlines the process for taxing railroad and bridge companies within school districts. It explicitly states that the provisions of the law do not apply to colored school districts. However, it mandates that the same rate of taxation assessed against railroad and bridge companies in white graded or common school subdistricts shall also be assessed against all taxable property in such districts. The collected railroad and bridge taxes are to be paid to the county superintendent and then apportioned between white and colored common school districts located within the same boundary, based on the ratio of white to colored children of pupil age residing in the district.

laws.summary: This section of the Kentucky Statutes from 1922 outlines the structure of common school districts, stating that each county shall compose a school district, with an exception for cities or towns that maintain a separate system of public schools. The remaining portion of the county outside such city or town district would then constitute a school district. The text also includes provisions regarding the examination and certification of teachers, including penalties for cheating and unlawful possession of examination questions. Additionally, it references case law related to school boards, taxes, and the validity of school acts. Notably, one of the cited cases, 'Grady v. Larue Co. Board, 149 Ky. 49; 147 S. W. 928', explicitly mentions 'Separate schools for white and colored.'

laws.summary: This statute outlines the organization and duties of school trustees and division boards in Kentucky. It details the election of trustees, the formation of division boards, the role of the county superintendent, and the process for filling vacancies. A significant portion of the text focuses on the census of school-aged children, including illiterate children and those attending school outside their district. Notably, it includes a section (§ 4434a-4) that was repealed and replaced by other sections, but the original text of this repealed section mentions 'the visitor of a colored school'.

laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 4437, pp. 2439–2440
laws.summary: This statute outlines the process for electing a visitor for colored schools within a subdistrict. It specifies that such an election shall be held, with nominations and elections conducted similarly to subdistrict trustees, but with the crucial distinctions that nominating petitions must be signed by colored voters, and only colored voters are eligible to vote for the visitor. The visitor's duties for the colored school are identical to those of subdistrict trustees, with the exception of not being a member of the division board. The statute also references a court case validating the appointment of a visitor for colored schools.

laws.title: § 4439a. Seminary property may be acquired by county board of education.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 4439a, p. 2441
laws.summary: This statute allows county boards of education or boards of trustees of white graded common school districts to acquire county seminary property. The statute specifies that if such property is acquired, it or its proceeds must be used for the benefit of all white pupils in the county, ensuring they are made whole for their interest in the seminary property. This implies a segregation of educational benefits based on race.

laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 4464, pp. 2449–2450
laws.summary: This statute outlines the process for establishing graded common school districts. It specifies requirements for petitions, elections, and taxation. Crucially, it mandates that elections to establish these districts are for 'legal white voters' and that any taxes levied are on 'white voters or corporations' or a poll tax on 'each white male inhabitant'. It also requires that graded common schools operate a high school of equal rank or pay tuition for eligible pupils to attend county or public high schools.

laws.summary: This statute outlines the process for converting an ordinary common school district into a free graded school district. It details the legislative provision for such conversions, the payment of the common school fund, and the requirements for elections to establish these graded schools. Notably, it includes a provision stating that the property of white persons must be taxed for white schools and that of colored persons for colored schools, indicating a legally mandated segregation in education.

laws.summary: This statute explicitly outlines the establishment of graded common schools for colored people, mirroring the provisions for white districts. It mandates racial segregation in these schools, prohibiting white individuals from voting in colored school elections, taxing white property for colored schools, taxing colored property for white schools, and preventing inter-racial attendance at these segregated institutions.

laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 4481, pp. 2458–2459
laws.summary: This statute outlines the process for graded common school districts to issue bonds for school purposes. It details the authorization for the board of trustees to call elections, appoint officers, and canvass returns. Crucially, it states that if the purpose of the bond issue is to erect buildings for white graded schools, colored voters are not entitled to vote, as their property will not be subject to taxation for these buildings or schools, nor can their children attend. The statute also specifies voting procedures, notice requirements, and the composition of election officers.

laws.title: § 4487. The provision in regard to the apportionment of railroad taxes bet ween white and colored schools has no application to the tax upon any other corporation.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 4487, p. 2462
laws.summary: This section of the Kentucky Statutes from 1922, specifically §4487, discusses the apportionment of railroad taxes between white and colored schools. It states that an agreement between trustees of white and colored schools for apportionment is a nullity and that taxes imposed on railroad companies must be apportioned between schools for white and colored children of the city. Other sections in this excerpt deal with the issuance of bonds for graded schools and tax collection.

laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 6, p. 2469
laws.summary: This statute mandates that in all examinations for state and elementary certificates, applicants be assigned numbers instead of using their names. The county superintendent is to keep a record of these numbers and names and forward a copy to the state superintendent. The purpose is to ensure grading and certification are based on merit alone. However, it explicitly states that the only distinction made between the manuscripts of white and colored teachers shall be the use of numerals for white teachers and letters of the alphabet for colored teachers. Violation is a misdemeanor.
key_provisions: § 6.) § 4501a -7. Papers to be numbered .- In all examinations for state certificates, and elementarycertificates,the applicantsshall be givennumbers by the countysuperin- tendentwhichnumbersshallbeplaceduponthe papers instead of names . The county superintendent shallkeep a record in his office of such numbers and names and for- ward a copy of the same in a separate en- velope by registeredmail to the statesuper- intendent. In gradingpapersand incerti- fying to the state superintendent the re- sultsof such examinations, the numbers must be used ; nor shallthe names be dis- closedto any one except to the persons mak- ingoutthecertificates. The purposeofthis law shallbe to insure that allpapers shall be graded , and certificatesissued upon merit alone. The violationof this law by any person whatever shallconstitutea mis- demeanor , and be punishable by a fine of not lessthan twenty-fivedollars($25.00), nor more than one hundred dollars ($100.00) in each case. The only distine- tion that shall be made between the manu- scriptsof the white and colored teachers shall be that the numerals shall be used for the white teachers and lettersof the alpha- bet in alphabetical order for the colored teachers. (Id., § 7.)

laws.title: § 4522. Donation or devise to; by whom held.
laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 4522, p. 2476
laws.summary: This statute prohibits the maintenance or operation of any college, school, or institution where both white and Negro races are received as pupils for instruction. It imposes fines on individuals or corporations violating this provision. It also makes it unlawful for instructors to teach in such integrated institutions and for individuals of one race to attend a school where the other race is taught, with exceptions for penal institutions. The law also allows for separate branches of private institutions for different races, provided they are at least twenty-five miles apart.

laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 4535a-1, pp. 2483–2484
laws.summary: This section of the Kentucky Statutes from 1922 details appropriations for the Kentucky Normal and Industrial Institute for colored persons and establishes two state normal school districts (eastern and western) for white populations. It also outlines the objects of these schools, which is to train teachers for common branches and the art of teaching. A specific statute (§ 4535) authorizes the board to grant certificates and diplomas to students who complete prescribed courses, with diplomas entitling them to teach in colored common schools.

laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 4535a-25, pp. 2487–2488
laws.summary: This statute outlines the appointment process for students to normal schools in Kentucky. It specifies that each county is entitled to appoint one white pupil for every 500 white school children (or fraction thereof over 250). The selection process involves the county superintendent examining applicants based on qualifications and character. The statute also includes a provision that pupils appointed must sign a declaration to teach in public schools for a specified period, or they will be required to pay tuition. This implies a system of racial segregation in educational appointments.

Crucially, it specifies that each county is entitled to appoint 'one white pupil for every three thousand, and one for each fraction thereof over fifteen hundred of white school children'. This explicit racial classification for educational opportunities is a hallmark of Jim Crow legislation.

laws.citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 4758-7, pp. 2598–2599
laws.summary: This statute defines vagrancy and outlines penalties, including fines and mandatory labor on public works. It specifies that the inability to obtain work or the possession of sufficient funds is not a defense. The law also establishes prima facie evidence of vagrancy for individuals who loiter, are addicted to intoxicants, are professional gamblers, or are supported by the labor of others. Enforcement duties are assigned to various law enforcement officers, with penalties for failure to enforce.

laws.summary: This section of the Kentucky Common School Laws from 1896 outlines the distribution of the school fund, stating that no distinction shall be made on account of race or color in distributing the fund, but mandates separate schools for white and colored children. It also details how surplus funds are handled and the use of federal tax refund money for educational purposes.

laws.citation: Kentucky Common School Laws., 1896, § 41, pp. 30–31
laws.summary: This statute outlines the responsibilities and powers of county superintendents in Kentucky's common school system. It details election procedures, bond requirements, and the superintendent's authority to lay off, abolish, or consolidate school districts, condemn unfit schoolhouses and furniture, and make official visits. Notably, it includes a provision for counties with a city of the first class maintaining a separate school system, stating that the county superintendent must reside outside such city and be elected by voters residing outside the city. This implies a potential for separate educational systems based on urban/rural distinctions, which could have been used to segregate Black students if such separate systems were racially divided.

It specifies that county certificates shall be granted to persons not under eighteen years of age upon written examinations. Each school districtshall be under the control of three trustees,

schools,able to read and write,ifpracticable,one of whom shallbe

of any private school shall be eligibleto hold the officeof trustee
of any common school. The vote in electinga trusteeshallbe taken
viva voce, and the electionshall be held at the schoolhouse, and if
no schoolhouse be in the district, at such convenient place as the
trustees may select, from one o'clocktillsix o'clockin the after-
noon on the firstSaturday of June in each year,noticethereof hav-
ing been posted by the trustees at three of the most public places
in the districtfor ten days immediately preceding the day of
election. At this election the qualified voters of the district
shall be the electors; and any widow having a child between six
and twenty -years of age, and any widow or spinsterhaving a ward
between the ages of six and twenty years may also vote. The
officersof the electionshall be a judge and a clerk, who shall be
residentsof the district,and be chosen by the voters at the opening
of the polls. The judge of electionshall give the casting vote in
case of a tie, provided he has not heretofore voted , and give a cer-
tificateof electionto the person elected, signed by himself, and
report the trusteesthus elected,in writing, to the county superin-
tendent of the county within fivedays afterthe day of election. In
case of a tie, in which the judge has voted, then he shall certify
the fact to the county superintendent, and the county superinten-
dent shall appoint the trustee, and give him a certificate, and the
trustee so selectedshall act until his successor is duly qualified.
The trustee so elected shall hold officefor three years , from the
firstday of July succeeding his election, and untilhis successor is
duly elected or appointed and qualified. Any two of the trustees
may constitutea quorum to transactthe businesspertainingto their
office, at a meeting of which all shall have had reasonable notice.

meetings , and to make the reports, and to perform all other such
acts and dutiesas required by law of trustees;and in case of neglect

ject to like finesand penalties as imposed by law on trustees for

wise impair the tenure of officeof trustees who have been duly
elected or appointed under the present school law .

laws.summary: This statute explicitly mandates the segregation of public schools based on race. It states that provisions for graded common schools apply to districts organized by colored people, with the word 'colored' replacing 'white' where applicable. Crucially, it prohibits white individuals from voting in elections for colored schools, prevents the taxation of white property for colored schools, and vice versa. It also forbids white children from attending colored schools and colored children from attending white schools.

In that case the word "colored" is to be substituted for the word " white " whenever it has occurred heretoforein thislaw . laws.summary: This statute outlines the enforcement of compulsory school attendance laws. It details penalties for parents or guardians who fail to ensure their children attend school, including fines and legal action. Crucially, Section 164 explicitly states that the conditions and provisions of the act apply to parents, guardians, or persons having control of colored children in the same manner as white children. However, it also includes a segregation clause: 'but no white child shall be permitted to attend or become a pupil in any school for colored children, and no colored child shall be'. This section directly mandates racial segregation in schools.

laws.summary: This act appropriates funds for the Kentucky Institute for Deaf Mutes and mandates the admission of colored deaf and dumb pupils on the same terms as white pupils. It specifies that the colored department will receive the same per capita support and an additional annual appropriation for officers and teachers. Crucially, it states that both races will be under the same management and superintendent, with the board of commissioners for the white institution overseeing the colored department. It also notes that existing officers and employees will not receive additional pay for services to colored mutes.

laws.summary: This statute outlines the process for assessing and collecting taxes from railroad companies for common school districts. Section 6 explicitly states that the provisions of this law shall not be construed to apply to any colored school district, thereby creating a separate and unequal system for funding education based on race. It mandates that taxes collected for white graded common school districts and white common school districts are to be distributed accordingly, while implicitly excluding colored school districts from these provisions.

laws.summary: This section contains abstracts of legal decisions and opinions related to Kentucky's common school laws. One abstract states that the school fund can only be applied to schools taught by qualified teachers in legally laid out districts, under elected trustees, which all white children within a specified age are privileged to attend. Another abstract, however, asserts that all legislation discriminating against any race or class violates the US Constitution, and state taxation for education should apply to all classes and races equally, with all children entitled to an equal share of the common school fund.

The common -school sys- tem provided for by the Constitution was intended to be general, governed and aided in allparts of the State in the same way

visions,therefore,an emergency exists,and thisact shalltake effect

Approved March 22,1892 .
APPENDIX .
Abstracts of Decisions of the Court of Appeals and of the
Superior Court Bearing on the Common School
Laws ; also of Attorney -General's Opinions .
1. Power of State to Establish Common School Systems. The
power of the States to establishand maintain systems of common
schools,to raisemoney for that purpose by taxation,and to govern ,
control and regulate such schools when established, is one of
"the powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitu-
tuition,nor prohibited by itto the States," and consequently it is
reserved to the States respectively,or to theirpeople. 1874. Mar-
shallvs.Donovan ,& c.,10 Bush ,690.
2. "What are Common Schools ?"-The school fund can not be
applied by the Legislature to any schools except those actually
taught by teachers qualifiedaccording to law to teach in districts
laid out by authority of the school laws , and under the control of
trusteeselected under those laws , which all white children in the
districtwithin a specifiedage are privilegedto attend. 1874. Col-
lins vs.Henderson , & c., 11 Bush , 74.
Common -School System to be General. The common -school sys-
tem provided for by the Constitution was intended to be general,
governed and aided in allparts of the State in the same way , and
to the same extent. 1878. Auditor vs.Holland , & c.,14 Bush ,152.
Constitutional Law - Discrimination Against Negroes- Taxa-
tion. All legislationwhich discriminates against any particular
race or class of persons is in violationof the Constitution of the
United States. Therefore, State taxation for the purposes of edu-
cation should be provided for by general laws , applicable to all
classesand racesalike,allthe childrenof the Statebeing entitled
to an equal share of the proceeds of the "Common School Fund ,"
and of allState taxation for the purposes of education.
An act,entitled"An act to establisha uniform system of com
mon schools for the colored children of this Commonwealth ," ap-
proved February 23,1874,isunconstitutional,because,by implica-
tion, itexcludes the negro children of the State from any share of
the proceeds of the "Common School Fund " set apart by the Consti-
tution, as well as from the annual tax levied on the property of
white persons for school purposes. 1884. Dawson vs. Lee, Lee vs.
Hill, 83 Kentucky Reports ,49 .
5-1 . Particular Appropriation of Common School Fund was "in
aid of Common Schools."- An act of the Legislature converting a
common school districtinto a graded free school district, and pro-
viding for the payment of the graded free school of the pro rata of
the common school fund going to that common school district,is an
appropriation of the common school fund in aid of common
schools," and is,therefore,not in violationof that clause of the Con-
stitutionwhich provides that said fund shall not be appropriated
for any other purpose .
2. Submission of Question whether Graded School Should be Es-
tablished. Under such an act, which provided that the trustees
should take the sense of the voters as to whether the proposed
school should be established, the submission of the question as to
whether a tax should be leviedto establishand supporta graded
school was a substantialcompliance with the statute.
3. Same - Power of Trustees to fix Time of Election.-The statute
fixeda day for submitting the question to the voters, but further
provided that the trustees should have power to open a poll, not
oftener than once a year, upon the question of establishingthe
graded school, and for the election of trustees, until the same
should be adopted . Held - That the trustees had the power to fix
the time for holding any election after the firstone , provided they
did not open a poll oftener than once a year .
4. CurativeStatutes.-Any mere irregularitiesin the electionun-
der the statute,the Legislaturehad the power to cure by a subse-
quent statute ratifyingthe electionand the acts of the trustees
thereunder .
5. Same . A curativestatuteisvalid ifitmerely dispenses with
that which might have been dispensed with by the Legislature at
the outset, or ifittreatsas immaterialthat which the priorlaw
might have treated as immaterial. 1889. Williamstown Graded
Free School Districtvs. Webb , & c., 89 Kentucky Reports ,265.
6. Normal Schools.-No appropriationfor the support of normal
schools san be constitutionallymade out of the school fund . 1874.
Collinsvs.Henderson,& c.,11 Bush,75.
7. Appropriation not in aid of Common Schools.- An act appropri-
ating a part of the school fund for the purchase of Collin'sHistory
of Kentucky , for school districts, is not in aid of common schools,
and , therefore, unconstitutional. Ib.
8. Taxation. In general, taxation must be equal and uniform ,
but where the benefitsare special and peculiar, those alone who
receivethe benefitsmay be made to pay the tax. 1874. Marshall
vs.Donovan ,& c.,10 Bush ,691.
9. Taxation- Irregularityin Election. Where a tax in aid of
common schools has been imposed pursuant to an electionheld for
that purpose, the burden is on the tax-payer, who resiststhe col-
lectionof the tax, to show that itis void. A mere irregularityin
conducting the electionwill not authorize the chancellor to inter-
pose. 1881. Trustees,& c.,vs.Garvey ,MS .Opinion .
10. Definiteness. A tax of twenty -fivecents on the hundred dol-
lars is sufficientlydefinite. Ib.
11. School Tax - Notice of Vote.- It is not necessary that a notice
of the time and object of a vote upon a school tax should be signed
by allthe Trustees of the District. A signing by the Chairman of
the Board of "Trustees" is a signing by the trustees within the
meaning of the statute. 1886. Frederick vs. Ragland , 7 Ky . Law
Rep .,743.
12. Collectorof Tax .- The Sheriff is, under ordinary circums-
tances,the properofficerto collecta tax votedby a schooldistrict.
The provision of the statute that the Board of Trustees "may ap-
point a Collectorof Taxes ," does not mean that they shall appoint
a Collector . Ib .
13. Common Schools- Taxation . An act of the Legislature au-
thorizing a particular district to vote a tax in aid of the common
school fund ,in order that the school may be taught the entireyear,
or the higher branches of education brought within reach of allthe
children,isnot in violationof the Constitution, Stateor Federal.
Nor is the teaching of the higher branches of learning in violation
of the common school law of the State . 1887. Newman and Others
vs.Thompson ,9 Ky .Law Rep .,199.
14. Condemnation of Schoolhouse. A majority of the qualified
voters of a common school districthaving petitioned the school
commissioner to condemn the schoolhouse of the district as unfit
tobe occupiedfor the purpose of a common school,he was authorized
by statuteto condemn it,and the trustees,upon being notifiedof the
condemnation by the commissioner , were authorized to order the
collection of a tax for the erection of a new schoolhouse without sub-
mitting the question to the qualifiedvoters of the district. 1885.
Bishop vs.Route ,7 Ky . Law Rep .,962 .
15-1 . Selectionof sitefor Schoolhouseand Levy of Tax . If the
siteof a schoolhouse is not located by the trustees of a common
school district,as the law directs,a majority of the electorsmay ap-
peal to the county superintendent, whose decisionis final; and as
lessthan a majority of the electorscan not even appeal,itis quite
clearthat they can not,on the ground that the siteis not where it
should be, enjoin a tax levied by the trustees.
2. Two Trustees are a quorum ,and their act is the act of the Board .
-Therefore ,where three trusteessigned an order of levy, the fact
that one of them did so under a mistake of law does not invalidate
the order .
3. Conditions Precedent to right to order Levy .--Selection of a site
for a schoolhouse and obtaining a titleare not conditions precedent
to the rights to order a levy. 1889. Stiles,& c., vs. Beall. & c., 11
Ky . Law Rep .,486.
16-1 . Selectionof Sitefor Schoolhouse- Powers of County Super-
intendent. The countysuperintendentof schools,in hearingan ap-
peal from the decision of the trustees of a school district in the se-
lectionof a sitefor a schoolhouse, acts in a judicialcapacity, and,
likeother judicialofficers, may reconsiderhis judgment if it is
made manifest to him that it is erroneous, provided it is done
within a reasonable time,and before rights have been acquired un-
der his previous decision.
2. Same . The decisionof the county superintendentis con-
clusive,and can not be disturbed by court except upon the ground
that he was influencedby improper motives. 1890. Brinsore vs.
Cottenham ,& c.,Ky .Law Rep .,720 .
17. Collection of Tax to Build a School -house , etc.- 1 . Under the
present school law the trustees of a common school districtmay
order the collection of a tax to build or repair a school -house with
out submitting the question to the voters of the district,but itis a
conditionprecedent of the right to order the tax that is necessary
to build a school-house , or that the county superintendent has con-
demned the school-house ,and that itneeds repairing.
2. The Legislaturehas the constitutionalpower to authorize the
trustees of a school districtto order the collectionof a tax, not to
exceed a certainsum ,without submitting the question to a popular
vote. While the Legislaturemust always prescribethe rule under
which the taxation is imposed , and can not referthis power to an-
other body , yet having prescribed the rule it need not fixthe ex-
act sum to be raised or the particularsof the expenditure. 1889.
Macklin,& c.,vs.TrusteesCommon SchoolDistrictNo. 9,ofFrank-
linCounty ; 88 Ky .Reports ,597.
18.Towns and Cities- Finesand Forfeitures- Common Schools.-
Under an amendment of January 12,1860,to the charter of the town
ofHarrodsburg ,providing that the finesand forfeituresrecovered in
the name of the Commonwealth in the police court of the town
should be vested in the board of trusteesfor the use of the common
schools in the town , the town and not the common schools was en
titledto allfinesor forfeituresarisingfrom a violationof town ordi-
nances, whether imposed in the name of the Commonwealth or in
the name of the town . 1887. Board of Trustees of the town of
Harrodsburg vs.Harrodsburg Educational District, 9 Ky . Law
Rep ., 605.
19. School Commissioner.--Mandamus is the proper remedy
againstthe county judge for refusingto permit school commis-
sionerto qualify. 1883. Greenup County Court, & c., vs.Clifton
5 Kentucky Law Rep .,241 .
20. Suretiesof Commissioner. The suretiesof a Commissioner
are not responsiblefor money drawn from the treasury by him un-
lessitis drawn according to law . 1872. Hammond vs. Crawford ,
& c.,9 Bush ,77.
21. Trustees- Employment of Teachers.- School trustees have
the right to act untiltheirsuccessorsare chosen and qualified. One
of two trustees elected in room of two whose term had expired,
declined to qualify; the other qualified,but the commissioner fail-
ing toreceivetheevidenceofhisqualification,appointedtwo others
in their stead. Held- That a teacher employed by two of
the former Trustees, and the newly elected Trustee who had been
qualified, was entitledto the schoolmoney ,and not a teacherem-
ployed by the Trusteesappointedby the Commissioner, and there
being an old school-house and a new ,it isimmaterial that the
former taught in the old house and the latter in the new . 1884 .
Cravens vs.Purns ,by ,& c.,5 Ky .Law Rep .,602 .
22. Suit by Trustees. The Trustees of a school districtas such,
may maintain an actionforthe recoveryof schoolproperty,but it
isproper that they should give theirnames . 1884. Lewis vs.Trus
tees,& c.,5 Ky .Law Rep .,767 .
23. School Property.- Trustees of a school districtcan not main-
tain an action to recover a piece of ground given to build a school-
house upon forthe benefitof the neighborhood,a buildinghaving
been erected by the neighbors and used as a school-house . The
patrons of the school,or one,for all,must sue. Ib.
24. Payment of Teachers. The collectionof the amount neces
sary to be raised,in additionto the public funds for the payment of
teachers ,must be provided for by the Trustees by contribution from
the patrons or otherwise ; and if the Trustees fail to make this pro-
vision,they are personallyliableto the teacher for the amount they
had agreed to pay him . The teacher should have nothing to do
with the raisingthis fund . 1867. Ferguson vs.True ,& c.,3 Bush ,
257 .
25. Trustee Compelled to make Report .- The teacher of a district
school may by mandamus compel the Trustee to make to the Com-
missioner the report necessary to enable the teacher to get his
wages from the State. The fact that the Trustee may be indicted
for a failureto report, and is liablein damages to any one injured
by the failure, does not exclude the remedy by mandamus . 1885.
Jones,& c.,vs.Strange,MS .Opinion .
26. Evidence of Teacher'sEmployment .- When a school has been
taught as a free school by a person claiming to have been properly
employed ,actuallyattended by nearly allof the childrenin the dis-
trict, visitedand recognized as the common school by one Trustee
without any active opposition from another, the evidence adduced
to prove the employment shouldnot be subjectedto the most rigid
and exhaustive analysis. Ib.
27. Attachments of Teacher's Salary .-Money due a common
11
school teacher can not be attached in hands of Commissioner . 1871 .
Tracy ,& c.,vs.Hornbuckle ,& c.,8 Bush ,336. 1879. Allen,& c.,vs.
Russell,& c.,78 Ку .116.
28. Suit Against Trustees.- In a suit by a teacher against Trus-
teesalleginga contract with all,no recovery can be had upon proof
of a contract made with part only. 1885. Houngan , & c., vs. Phil-
lips,7 Ky . Law Rep .,150.
29. Power ofLegislatureoverSchoolFund .-The GeneralAssem-
bly has no power to devote any portion of the school fund to the
payment of teachers not acting under the controlor supervision of
the officersof the common schools. 1872. Halbert vs. Sparks , 9
Bush ,262 .
30. The Legislaturecan make a school district,and impose a tax
forschool purposes,without submitting the question to a vote of the
people thereof. Fitzpatrickvs. Board of Trustees of Mt. Sterling
Public School District,87 Ky .Reports ,132 .
1
31. Graded Schools. Under the law , approved May 4, 1888, a
majority of white voters in any districtmust vote for the tax to
make itlawful. A majorityof thosevotingisnot sufficient. (The
law isdifferentsinceJuly 6,1893,and requiresonly a majorityof
thosevoting.) Kate Riggs vs. Stephens , Co. Supt .;and Garvey vs.
Dulaney , Ky .Appellate Court , Dec. 17, 1891.
32. Taxation .---Trustees must make a record of all taxes levied
when the levy is ordered, and make a record of every step taken .

from the common school districtas would pay tuition,and then col-

suitable house . The order of condemnation need not even be
entered on his record before the levy of the tax ismade ;itis suffici-
ent ifdone later. The county superintendent isthe judge as to the

laws.citation: Kentucky Common School Laws., 1896, p. 171
laws.summary: This statute addresses district taxation for school purposes in the Robards District. A special act authorized a tax of 75 cents per $100 of property value and $5 per poll to erect buildings and maintain a ten-month school. The act explicitly states it does not apply to negroes or their property, though white taxpayers could not complain on this basis. The statute also details requirements for notice posting, the object of the vote, and the need for a trustee order designating the tax amount, even if not formally recorded.

laws.citation: Kentucky Common School Laws., 1896, p. 175
laws.summary: This case addresses the collection of delinquent taxes owed to school districts. It states that taxes due before November 11, 1892, are to be collected by trustees, while taxes due after that date must be collected by the county superintendent. Crucially, the ruling states that a corporation cannot avoid taxation by claiming it has no color, as all property is taxed except that belonging to colored people. This explicitly indicates a racially discriminatory tax exemption.

laws.summary: This section of the Kentucky Common School Laws from 1900 outlines the distribution of school funds and mandates separate schools for white and colored children. It states that no distinction shall be made on account of race or color in distributing the school fund, but separate schools for white and colored children shall be maintained. It also addresses the use of funds from the United States and prohibits the appropriation of educational funds for church or sectarian schools.

laws.summary: This statute outlines the process for examining and certifying county superintendents. It details the examination procedures, the roles of various officials, and the qualifications for the office. Notably, it includes a provision stating that in counties with a separate school system for a first-class city, no person shall be eligible to be county superintendent other than a resident of the county outside of such city or town. This implies a segregation of school systems and potential exclusion based on residency within a segregated system.

§ 63. [Dutiesof Stateand CountyBoardsas to Questions, Examina-
tions, Certificates.]- County certificates shall be granted
by the county board of examiners to persons not under
eighteen years of age, upon written examinations upon the
science and art of teaching, and upon the subjectsembraced
in the common school course, including, in connection with
physiologyand hygiene, the effectsof alcoholicdrinks and
narcoticsupon the human system ,held in each county of the
State for white teachers upon the third Friday and Saturday
in May ,June ,July and August ,of each year,and for colored
teachers upon the fourth Friday and Saturdays of the same
months ;and no examinations shallbe held at any other time
whatever . No certificateshall be issued upon the days of ex-
amination ;nor shallany answers be passed upon in the pres-
ence of any applicant. The State Board of Examiners shall
carefully prepare four series of questions for white teachers ,
and an equal number for colored teachers, all of the same
grade ; shall enclose in a separate envelope such number of
questions of each given seriesas the county superintendent

amination, with the name of the subjectplainlywrittenor
printed across the seal thereof ; shall enclose the several envel-
opes in a package , which they shallseal and forward by reg-
isteredmail or by express to each county superintendent at
least two weeks before the examination , designating the

tendent shallcarefullypreserve the said package of questions

said package shallthen be examined by the other examiners

opened in their presence. Immediately after examining the

der his oath as examiner ,upon blanks furnished for that pur-
pose by the Superintendent of Public Instruction,give a sepa-
rate certificate, with the signature attested by two reliable
witnesses,that he had personallyinspected the said package ,
and whether he had found the same intact,as provided herein,
and forward the certificateto the Superintendent of Public

sonable time for the examination upon each subject, taking
the subjectsin the order named in the sectionspecifyingthe

lect the answers of all the applicants when the time allotted
has expired;and ,afterthe firstsubjectispresented to the ap-
plicants, the said examiners shallnot present any other sub-

swers of allapplicantsto allquestions previously presented.

are fully satisfied that said applicant possesses an unexcep-

and ,in no event,shall a certificatebe granted to any person
who indulges in drunkenness , profanity, gambling or licen-
tiousness,or who , within the beliefof the examiners ,has had

during the examination , exclude from the room all persons
other than applicants,see that the applicantsare seated at a
proper distancefrom each other,and shallsee that no assist-
ance is given or obtained by any applicant during the exam-
ination,and shallrefuseto grant a certificateto any applicant
who may either obtain or give such assistance. The county
superintendent, and at leastone of the examiners, shallbe
present , and shall conduct all examinations and sign all cer-

shallhave fullpower , and it shall be their duty to make in-
vestigationas to the moral character of applicants; and the

ter an oath as to improper use of questions, and as to other
matters touching the qualificationsof teachers under this act.

laws.citation: Kentucky Common School Laws., 1900, § 100, pp. 70–71
laws.summary: This statute outlines the process for establishing a graded common school district. It requires a written petition from at least ten legal voters who are taxpayers in a justice's district, town, or city of the fifth or sixth class. The county judge is to order an election to gauge the sentiment of legal white voters on the proposition of levying an annual tax (ad valorem and/or poll tax) to maintain the school and its facilities. The tax is limited to 50 cents per $100 of property and $1.50 per capita for white male inhabitants over 21.

laws.summary: This statute explicitly mandates the segregation of graded common schools based on race. It states that provisions for graded common schools apply to districts organized by colored people, with the word 'colored' to be substituted for 'white'. It prohibits white persons from voting in colored school elections, taxing white property for colored schools, taxing colored property for white schools, and prevents children of one race from attending schools organized for the other race.

laws.citation: Kentucky Common School Laws., 1900, § 151, pp. 96–97
laws.summary: This section of the Kentucky Common School Laws from 1900 outlines provisions for the education of "colored children." It details the disposition of donations for their education, the age range for pupil-children (six to twenty years), and the census-taking process, which is to be conducted in the same manner as for white children. It also specifies that colored school districts will be designated by letters and that colored school trustees will be elected similarly to white trustees. Crucially, it states that no tax shall be levied upon white persons or their property for the benefit of colored schools, nor shall any services be required of white persons for this purpose. Conversely, it implies that taxes and services for colored schools would be levied upon and required from the Black community.

laws.summary: This section of the Kentucky Common School Laws from 1900 outlines provisions for the education of "colored children." It details the disposition of donations for their education, the age range for pupil-children (six to twenty years), and the census-taking process, which is to be conducted in the same manner as for white children. It also specifies that colored school districts will be designated by letters and that colored school trustees will be elected similarly to white trustees. Crucially, it states that no tax shall be levied upon white persons or their property for the benefit of colored schools, nor shall any services be required of white persons for this purpose. Conversely, it implies that taxes and services for colored schools would be levied upon and required from the Black community.

laws.summary: This statute outlines the organization and funding of public schools in fourth-class cities. It establishes a board of education with powers to manage school libraries, purchase textbooks for indigent children, and admit out-of-city pupils with tuition fees. Crucially, it mandates that the Superintendent of Public Instruction allocate funds from the common school fund to a 'white board of education' for white children and a 'colored board of education' for colored children, based on per capita amounts for each child of pupil age in the district. This explicitly establishes a racially segregated system for school funding.

laws.citation: Kentucky Common School Laws., 1900, § 6, p. 149
laws.summary: This statute outlines the process for assessing and collecting taxes from railroad companies within common school districts. Crucially, Section 6 explicitly states that the provisions of this law shall not apply to any colored school district. It then mandates that railroad taxes collected in a district shall be distributed between white common school districts and any colored common school districts located within the same boundary, based on the ratio of white to colored children of pupil age. This establishes a racially segregated system for the distribution of educational funds derived from railroad taxes.
key_provisions: § 6. The provisions of this law shall not be construed to apply to any coloredschool district: Provided,That the same rate of taxation assessed against the real estate of any rail- road company or corporation in any graded common school districtor common schooldistrict,in any year,shallbe assess- ed against allthe taxable property in such district, and the railroadtax, when collected,shallbe paid over to the county superintendent of the county in which the districtschoolhouse wherein the tax assessed shall be situated, and shall consti- tute and be held by the county superintendent as a graded or common district school fund ; and the said fund shall be ap- portioned and distributed by the county superintendent between the white graded common school or white common school districtwherein said tax shall be collected, and any colored common school district which shall be located over the same boundary ; the distribution shall be in the ratio that the whole number of white childrenof pupil age and the whole number of coloredchildrenof pupil age residingin the district shallbear to the whole number of children,white and colored, residing in the districtwherein such tax shall be collected.

APPENDIX .
Abstracts of Decisions of the Court of Appeals and of the
Superior Court Bearing on the Common School
Laws ; also of Attorney -General's Opinions .
1. " What are Common Schools ?"- The school fund can not
be applied by the Legislatureto any schools except those act-
ually taught by teachers qualified according to law to teach
indistrictslaidout by authorityof the school laws,and under
the control of trustees elected under those laws , which all
white children in the districtwithin a specifiedage are priv-
ilegedto attend. 1874. Collinsv.Henderson ,& c.,11 Bush ,74.
2. Power of Trusteesto fixTime of Electionfor Grade Com-
mon School. The statutefixeda day for submitting the ques-
tion to the voters, but further provided that the trustees
should have power to open a poll, not oftener than once a
year, upon the question of establishingthe graded school,
and for the election of trustees, until the same should be
adopted. Held - that the trustees had the power to fix
the time for holding any electionafterthe firstone, provided
they did not open a poll oftener than once a year . 83 Ken-
tucky Reports , 49 .
3. Curative Statutes.-Any mere irregularitiesin the elec-
tion under the statutethe Legislaturehad the power to cure
by a subsequent statuteratifyingthe electionand the acts of
the trustees thereunder .
4. Same . A curative statute is valid if it merely dis-
penses with that which might have been dispensed with by
the Legislature at the outset,or ifittreatsas immaterial that
which the priorlaw might have treated as immaterial. 1889.
Williamstown Graded Free School Districtv. Webb , & c., 89
Kentucky Reports,265.
[ 10 ]
5. Normal Schools.- No appropriation for the support of
normal schools can be constitutionally made out of the school
fund. 1874. Collinsv.Henderson ,& c.,11 Bush ,75.
6. Taxation.- In general, taxation must be equal and uni-
form , but where the benefitsare specialand peculiar, those
alone who receivethe benefitsmay be made to pay the tax.
1874. Marshall v.Donovan ,& c.,10 Bush ,691.
7. Taxation- Irregularityin Election.---Where a tax in aid
of common schools has been imposed pursuant to an elec-
tion held for that purpose, the burden is on the tax-payer,
who resiststhe collectionof the tax, to show that it is void.
A mere irregularityin conducting the election will not
authorizethe chancellorto interpose. 1881. Trustees,& c.,v .
Garvey , MS . Opinion .
8. Definiteness. A tax of twenty -fivecents on the hundred
dollarsis sufficientlydefinite. Ib.
9. School Tax- Notice of Vote. It is not necessary that a
notice of the time and object of a vote upon a school tax
should be signed by allthe Trustees of the District. A sign-
ing by the Chairman of the Board of "Trustees" is a signing
by the trustees within the meaning of the statute. 1886 .
Frederick v.Ragland ,7 Ky . Law Rep .,743.
10. Common Schools- Taxation . An act of the Legislature
authorizing a particular district to vote a tax in aid of the
common school fund , in order that the school may be taught
the entireyear, or the higher branches of education brought
within reach of all the children, is not in violationof the
Constitution , State or Federal . Nor is the teaching of the
higher branches of learning in violation of the common school
law of the State . 1887. Newman and others v . Thompson ,
9 Ky . Law Rep ., 199 .
If11-1 . Selectionof Sitefor Schoolhouseand Levy of Tax .
the site of a schoolhouse is not located by the trustees of a
common school district, as the law directs, a majority of the
electors may appeal to the county superintendent, whose
decisionis final; and as less than a majority of the electors
can not even appeal, it is quite clear that they can not on
the ground that the siteisnot where itshould be, enjoin a
tax levied by the trustees.
2. Two Trusteesare a quorum, and theiract is the act of the
Board . Therefore where three trustees signed an order of
levy, the fact that one of them did so under a mistake of law
does not invalidate the order .
3. ConditionsPrecedentto rightto order Levy. Selection of
a sitefor a schoolhouse and obtaining a titleare not condi-
tionsprecedentto the rightsto order a levy. 1889. Stiles,
& c.,v.Beall,& c.,11 Ky .Law Rep .,486.
12-1 . Selectionof Site for Schoolhouse- Powers of County
Superintendent. The county superintendent of schools, in
hearing an appeal from the decisionof the trusteesofa school
districtin the selectionof a sitefor a schoolhouse, acts in a
judicialcapacity, and ,like other judicialofficers, may recon-
siderhis judgment if it is made manifest to him that it is
erroneous, provided it is done within a reasonable time, and
beforerightshave been acquired under his previous decision.
2. Same . The decision of the county superintendent is
conclusive, and can not be disturbed by court except upon
theground that he was influencedby improper motives. 1890.
Brinsore v.Cottenham ,& c.,Ky . Law Rep .,720.
13. Collectionof Tax to Build a Schoolhouse, etc.- 1. Under
the present school law the trustees of a common school dis-
trictmay order the collection of a tax to build or repair a
schoolhouse without submitting the question to the voters
of the district, but itis a conditionprecedent of the right to
order the tax that it is necessary to build a schoolhouse , or
that the county superintendent has condemned the school-
house , and that it needs repairing .
2. The Legislature has the constitutional power to author-
ize the trustees of a school district to order the collection of
a tax, not to exceed a certain sum , without submitting the
question to a popular vote. While the Legislature must al-
ways prescribethe rule under which the taxation is imposed ,
and can not referthispower to another body ,yet having pre-
scribed the rule it need not fix the exact sum to be raised or
the particularsof the expenditure. 1889. Macklin , & c., v.
Trustees Common School District No. 9, of Franklin County ;
88 Ky .Reports,597.
14. Trustees- Employment of Teachers.- School trustees
have the right to act until their successors are chosen and
qualified. One of two trustees elected in room of two whose
term had expired declinedto qualify; the other qualified, but
the commissioner failing to receive the evidence of his quali
fication, appointed two others in their stead. Held- That a
teacher employed by two of the former Trustees, and the
newly electedTrustee who had been qualified, was entitled
10 the school money , and not a teacher employed by the
Trusteesappointedby the Commissioner, and therebeing an
old schoolhouse and a new , it is immaterial that the former
taught in the old house and the latter in the new . 1884 .
Cravens v.Purns ,by ,& c.,5 Ky . Law Rep ., 602.
15 , Suit by Trustees.--The trustees of a school district as
such may maintain an action for the recovery of school prop-
erty,but it is proper that they should give their names .
Lewis v.Trustees,& c.,5 Ky .Law Rep .,767.
1884 .
16. School Property.- Trustees of a school districtcan not
maintain an action to recover a piece of ground given to
build a schoolhouse upon for the benefitof the neighborhood ,
a building having been erected by the neighbors and used as
a schoolhouse. The patrons of the school,or one,for all,must
sue . Ib .
17. Payment of Teachers. The collection of the amount
necessary to be raised, in addition to the public funds for the
payment of teachers,must be provided for by the Trustees by
contribution from the patrons or otherwise ; and if the Trus-
tees failto make this provision, they are personally liable
to the teacher for the amount they had agreed to pay him .
The teacher should have nothing to do with the raisingof this
fund . 1867. Ferguson v.True ,& c., 3 Bush , 257.
18. Trustee Compelled to make Report .-The teacher of a dis-
trictschool may by mandamus compel the Trustee to make to
the Commissioner the report necessary to enable the teacher
to get his wages from the State . The fact that the Trustee
may be indictedfor a failureto report, and is liablein dam-
ages to any one injured by the failure, does not exclude the
remedy by mandamus . 1885. Jones , & c., v. Strange , MS .
Opinion .
19. Evidence of Teacher'sEmployment .- When a school has
been taught as a free school by a person claiming to have
been properly employed , actuallyattended by nearly allof the
children in the district, visitedand recognized as the com-
mon school by one Trustee without any active opposition
from another, the evidence adduced to prove the employ
ment should not be subjectedto the most rigidand exhaustive
analysis. Ib.
20. Attachments of Teacher'sSalary.---Money due a common
school teacher can not be attached in hands of Commissioner .
1871. Tracy, & c., v. Hornbuckle, & c., 8 Bush , 336. 1879.
Allen ,& c.,v.Russell,& c.,78 Ky .,116.
21. Suit Against Trustees. In a suit by a teacher against
Trustees alleginga contract with all,no recovery can be had
upon proof of a contract made with a part only. 1885.
Houngan ,& c.,v. Phillips,7 Ky . Law Rep ., 150.
22. Power of Legislatureover School Fund .-The General
Assembly has no power to devote any portion of the school
fund to the payment of teachers not acting under the con-
trol or supervision of the officersof the common schools . 1872 .
Halbert v.Sparks ,9 Bush ,262.
23. The Legislaturecan make a school district, and impose
a tax for schoolpurposes, without submittingthe question
to a vote of the people thereof. Fitzpatrick v. Board of
Trustees of Mt. Sterling Public School District, 87 Ky . Re-
ports , 132 .
24. Graded Schools.- Under the law , approved May 4, 1888,
a majority of white voters in any districtmust vote for
the tax to make it lawful. A majority of those voting is
not sufficient. (The law is differentsince July 6, 1893, and
requires only a majority of those voting.) Kate Riggs v.
Stephens , Co. Supt .;and Garvey v. Dulaney , Ky . Appellate
Court ,Dec. 17,1891.
25. Taxation .— Trustees must make a record of all taxes
levied when the levy is ordered, and make a record of every
step taken. Davidson v.Sterrett,Superior Court,March ,1892.
26. The Legislaturecan not Divert StateFund from a Common
School. A private academy was authorized to admit such
pupils from the common school districtas would pay tuition,
and then collect the pro rata of these pupils from State
school fund ; and also to exempt such persons as patronized
the academy from stricttaxation. Held.-That the act was
unconstitutionaland void. Underwood v. Wood , Co. Supt .,
Ky .Appellate Court,May 5,1892.
27. District Taxation . The trustees of a school district
need not seethe order of county superintendent in which he
condemns the house of their district. It is sufficient that
county superintendent notifies them as a condition warrant-
ing the levy of a tax to build a suitablehouse . The order of
condemnation need not even be entered on his record before
the levy of the tax is made ; it is sufficientif done later. The
county superintendent is the judge as to the need of a house
of furniture,and Trustees must act on noticefrom him . Trus-
tees of DistrictNo. 1, Barren County v. Jamison , Ky .Appel-
late Court,January 17, 1891.
28. District Taxation .- 1. No other assessment than that
made by the county assessor is needed in order to levy a dis-
trict tax .
2. The selectionof a site for the house , and securing a
fee-simple title, are not conditions precedent to the levy of
a tax, and house may be built on leased land, ifTrustees so
elect as for the best interests of the district .
3. The tax not being beyond that authorized by law , the
allegationthat itwould produce $170,and that only $80 was
needed to make the repairs, is not sufficientto justifythe
injunction. There being a differenceof opinion as to the
cost of repairs, the opinion of the trustees must control.
Cromwell v.Trustees Dis. No. 44, Franklin county, Superior
Court,June 8,1892.
29. Record Necessaryto Determine theDistrictin which a Tax
payerBelongs. A tax was voted in September ,1882 ; Mr. Bell
had acted as Trustee of the district in 1873 ; had sent his
childto school there as late as 1878; had , before 1873, asked
the County Superintendent to transfer him to said district,
and he thought he had been so transferred , but the County
Superintendent had never entered the change of boundary
on his record . When the tax was voted , Bell claimed not to
be in the district,and refused to pay the tax. Held- That he
never was in the district,and should not pay the tax. Abney
vs.Bell,Fleming County,SuperiorCourt,,Dec.16,1885.
30. District Taxation - Residence of Minor - Owner of Per-
sonalPropertySoughtto be Taxed.- 1 . The form of the order
in Trustee's Record and the form of the election notice need
not be preciselyidentical. It is sufficientthat they be the
same in substance .
2. The statutedoes not,in a case where an electionisheld
to vote a tax, and same has been voted, require the Trustees
thereafter to make and enter in their records a formal order
levying the tax voted. It is sufficientthat they make an
order appointing a collectorof the voted tax. The value of
the property in the district, as assessed by the County As-
sessor,isto be used for taxation by the district.
3. Part of the property taxed was a house and lot in
Princeton, Ky ., and in the districtwhere tax was levied;but
the greater part was stock, bonds and notes belonging to
minors and in the hands of a guardian in Louisville, Ken-
tucky. The parents of minors had livedin Princeton,but re-
moved to Texas , and thence to Tennessee , where they died ,
leaving three children. These children went to Princeton
where theirgrand parents lived. One had been sent to school
at Staunton ,Virginia,and had spent two vacations at Prince-
ton and one in Texas , where she was engaged to be married ;
the other two had remained at Princeton, and their property
had been taxed for State and county purposes in Princeton.
Held- That all three were citizens of Princeton district; and
all their property subject to taxation for school purposes.
Glover's Guardian vs. Princeton School District, Superior
Court, September ,1892.
31. DistrictTaxation to Enlarge School-house.- When it is
ascertained that a school -house is too small to accommodate
thechildrenofthe district,theCounty Superintendentcan re-
quire an addition to be made to it. No specificcourse is re-
quired to be followed by the Superintendent. His having
notified the trustees that the house was insufficient to ac-
commodate the children, and that they should make suitable
provisionfor their accommodation , was held to be sufficient.
Ratcliff,& c.,vs.Dist.No. 1,CaldwellCounty,SuperiorCourt,
September ,1892.
32. DistrictTaxation Under SpecialAct of Legislature.- A
tax of 75 cents on each $100 of property value, and $5 on each
poll to erect buildings and maintain ten months ' school in
the Robards Districthaving been voted by the whites, and
a collectorappointed, ten tax-papers proceeded to enjoin the
trustees and collector from collecting tax . Held- 1. The act
does not apply to negroes or their property, but the whites
can not complain on this account . 2. The notices having been

It also specifies that stock owned by colored persons in private corporations is taxable only for colored schools, and stock owned by white persons is taxable only for white schools. Agreements between white and colored school trustees for tax apportionment other than as required by law are deemed nullities.

Therefore, a corporation seeking exemption must prove its corporators and stockholders are black persons. It also clarifies that corporations are considered inhabitants for taxation purposes.

laws.citation: Kentucky Common School Laws., 1900, p. 167
laws.summary: This statute clarifies that school taxes levied on railroad property must also be levied on the property of white persons in the same district. It mandates the apportionment of railroad taxes between white and colored schools based on the proportion of colored pupil children to the total number of pupil children within the white district's boundaries. It also specifies that taxes on private corporations for graded schools are to be taxed only for the schools of the owner's race, and agreements for different apportionment methods are void.

Kentucky Statutes, providing for taxation of railroad prop-
erty for the benefitof school districts, it is plain that the
school tax upon railroad property can not be levied unless
taxes are leviedon the property of white persons in the same
district. It ismade the duty of the County School Superin-

fund as the number of colored pupil childrenresidingwithin
the boundary of the white districtbears to the number of
white and colored pupil children residing within said boun-
dary . (1889. Harrodsburg Educational District No. 28 vs.
Trustees of Colored School DistrictNo. 1,20th Ky . Law Rep .,
1487.)
52. Apportionment of Taxes Between White and Colored
Schools. The common school law provides that the railroad
tax shall be apportioned between the white and colored
schoolsin the same district,but thisprovisionhas no applica-
tion to the tax upon the property of any other corporation.

laws.title: Legal voters in election for establishing graded common school district
laws.citation: Kentucky Common School Laws., 1900, p. 172
laws.summary: This statute defines the legal voters eligible to establish a graded common school district under Section 4464 of the Kentucky Statutes. It specifies that voters must be white males over the age of twenty-one, with specific residency requirements in the state, county, and proposed district.
key_provisions: There seems to be no provision of law whereby a graded common school districtcan be diminished by taking therefrom any part of the territory once embraced therein . In other words , a graded common school districtmay be enlarged by extending its territoriallimits but can not be made smaller , territorially,by taking from itsoriginallimitsany part of the realestateoriginallyembraced therein. April ,1900 . ROBT .J. BRECKINRIDGE , XI . Attorney -General . 1 A person who has received a third class certificatecan not receive nor hold another third class certificate. August , 1900 . ROBT . J. BRECKINRIDGE , Attorney -General .

laws.citation: Kentucky Common School Laws, 1914, § 187, p. 11
laws.summary: This section of the Kentucky Constitution mandates that the school fund be distributed without distinction based on race or color, but requires separate schools to be maintained for white and colored children. It also outlines provisions for the use of funds received from the United States and prohibits the appropriation of educational funds for sectarian purposes. Additionally, it exempts school trustee elections from secret ballot requirements and sets municipal tax rates.
key_provisions: § 187. Each Race to Share Fund Equally - Separate Schools . In distributing the school fund no distinction shall be made on account of race or color and separate schools for white and colored children shall be maintained .
