statutes.summary: This section of the Kentucky Statutes from 1903, pertaining to Municipal Corporations of the Fourth Class, includes provisions related to schools. Specifically, it mentions the 'separation of white and black children' in the context of school buildings and teachers. This indicates a legally mandated segregation in educational facilities.

statutes.statute_citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, p. 1820
statutes.title: MUNICIPAL CORPORATIONS - FOURTH CLASS - Schools
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, p. 1820
statutes.summary: This section of the Kentucky Statutes from 1903 outlines the organization and operation of public schools within fourth-class municipal corporations. It details the powers and duties of the board of education, including the election of officers, control of school funds, curriculum, and the admission of children to schools. Notably, it includes a provision for the 'separation of white and black' children.

statutes.statute_citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, p. 1821
statutes.title: MUNICIPAL CORPORATIONS - Fifth Class - School law - common when not to affect
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, p. 1821
statutes.summary: This section of the Kentucky Statutes from 1903, specifically concerning Municipal Corporations of the Fifth Class, includes a reference to 'Separation of white and black pupils' under the 'School law' provisions. While the specific details of this separation are not provided in the excerpt, the explicit mention of separating pupils by race indicates a segregationist policy.

statutes.statute_citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, p. 192
statutes.title: PRESENT CONSTITUTION COMMONWEALTH OF KENTUCKY
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, p. 192
statutes.summary: This section of the Kentucky Constitution, from 1903, includes a provision for separate schools for white and colored pupils.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 1439
statutes.title: § 1439. Qualification of voters.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 1439, p. 623
statutes.summary: This statute outlines the qualifications for voters in Kentucky, specifying age, residency requirements, and exceptions. It lists persons convicted of treason, felony, bribery, or certain misdemeanors, those in confinement, and idiots and insane persons as ineligible to vote. It also notes that soldiers, seamen, and marines stationed in the state are not considered residents and cannot vote. Additionally, it states that payment of a poll-tax is a prerequisite for voting in municipal elections if required by the municipality's charter.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 1477
statutes.title: § 1477. Liability of judge for refusing vote.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 1477, pp. 640–642
statutes.summary: This statute outlines the oath required for individuals to vote in Kentucky elections. It details the residency requirements, disqualifications, and the process for administering and verifying the oath. It also establishes penalties for false swearing and mandates investigation by attorneys and the grand jury to identify and prosecute illegal voters. The enforcement mechanisms and the potential for discriminatory application, particularly in the context of historical voting restrictions for Black citizens, suggest a Jim Crow era characteristic.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 1487
statutes.title: § 1487. Officers of registration-- term and oath of office—non-attendance or vacancy supplied.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 1487, pp. 646–647
statutes.summary: This statute outlines the procedures for voter registration in cities, including the appointment and duties of registration officers, the process for challenging a person's right to register, the format of registration books, and the timing of registration. It specifies that registration books should include a column for 'Color'.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 1555
statutes.title: § 1555. Party affiliation—provisions for registering.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 1555, pp. 661–663
statutes.summary: This statute outlines the process for holding primary elections in Kentucky. It states that all legal voters have the right to participate, subject to additional political qualifications prescribed by the party committee. It also establishes a system for party affiliation registration, where individuals can declare their party preference on regular state registration books. While not explicitly mentioning race, this statute is classified as Jim Crow because the ability to impose 'additional political qualifications' by party committees, combined with the historical context of racial segregation in the South, allowed for the disenfranchisement of Black voters through discriminatory party rules and practices, effectively limiting their participation in the political process.

statutes.statute_citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 1, pp. 94–95
statutes.title: § 1.The General Assembly shall have no power to pass laws for the emancipation of slaves, without the consent of their owners, or without paying their owners, previous to such emancipation, a full equivalent in money, for the slaves so emancipated, and providing for their removal from the State.…
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 1, pp. 94–95
The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 1, pp. 93–94
statutes.summary: This section of the Kentucky Constitution outlines provisions related to slavery and free negroes/mulattoes. It grants the General Assembly power to regulate emancipation, prevent the immigration of free negroes and mulattoes who refuse to leave or return to the state, and punishes such individuals with felony charges and penitentiary confinement. It also addresses the prosecution of slaves for felony, stating that grand jury inquests are not necessary but petit jury trials are still a privilege. The text also includes provisions for the common school fund and the revision of the constitution.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 2008
statutes.title: § 2008. Appointment of board in counties having cities of first-class—terms of office.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 2008, pp. 824–825
statutes.summary: This statute establishes a Board of Children's Guardians in counties with a first-class city. The board is to be composed of six persons, two of whom shall be colored. The board will be a body politic and corporate, responsible for children's guardianship, and its members will be appointed by the judge of the city or police court.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 2095a
statutes.title: § 2095a. Houses of Reform - appropriation -payment of.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 2095a, pp. 850–856
statutes.summary: This statute outlines the operation of Houses of Reform for juveniles under eighteen. It details commitment duration, discharge procedures, educational and vocational instruction, the transfer of minor convicts from the penitentiary, and mandates the separation of white and colored inmates into distinct departments. It also includes provisions for funding and reporting.

statutes.title: § 250. Asylum unable to accommodate—patients may be received in another asylum.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 250, p. 280
The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 250, pp. 305–306
The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 1, 1915, § 250, pp. 308–309
The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 3, 1918, § 216b-26, p. 137
The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 250, p. 313
statutes.summary: This statute outlines the procedures for managing the capacity of insane asylums in Kentucky. It details how patient transfers are to be handled to prevent overcrowding and mandates that white and colored patients shall not be kept in the same buildings. It also addresses the reception of patients, the role of courts and superintendents, and provisions for discharged patients.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 282
statutes.title: § 282. Colored deaf mutes—institution for.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 282, p. 287
The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 282, p. 314
statutes.summary: This statute establishes a separate institution for the education of colored deaf mutes at Danville, Kentucky. It mandates that this institution be under the same board of commissioners as the institution for white deaf mutes, but explicitly states that the two races shall be forever kept entirely separate and distinct from each other.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 310
statutes.title: § 310. Appropriation—annual for colored children.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 310, p. 293
The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 3, 1918, § 310, p. 162
statutes.summary: This statute appropriates funds for the education of colored blind children in Kentucky, establishing a separate appropriation for their sole and exclusive use. It mandates that these funds be expended similarly to those for white blind children and that colored blind children receive equal terms of rights, benefits, and privileges. However, it also states that both races shall be under the same general management and superintendent.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 3219
statutes.title: § 3219. School tax.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 3219, pp. 1218–1220
statutes.summary: This statute mandates that the board of education shall provide, maintain, and support separate schools for colored children.

statutes.title: § 45274. Name of school—president and powers—superintendent.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 45274, p. 1604
The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 2, 1915, § 4527a, p. 905
Common School Laws of Kentucky, 1916, § 299, p. 140
The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 4527a, p. 2481
Baldwin's Kentucky Statute Service, 1922, § 4527a, pp. 802–803
statutes.summary: This statute details the renaming of the 'State Normal School for Colored Persons' to 'The Kentucky Normal and Industrial Institute for Colored Persons'. It outlines the powers and responsibilities of its board of trustees, the selection and duties of the institute's president, and the establishment of a department for agriculture and mechanics. It also specifies admission requirements for pupils, including a pledge to teach in colored common schools.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 4527
statutes.title: § 4527. Trustees—appointment—term of office—powers—vacancies—treasurer.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 4527, pp. 1603–1604
The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4527, pp. 1893–1894
The Common School Laws of Kentucky, 1910, § 419, p. 177
Kentucky Common School Laws, 1914, § 503, pp. 188–189
The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 2, 1915, § 4527, pp. 904–905
Common School Laws of Kentucky, 1916, § 290, p. 138
The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 3, 1918, § 4527, pp. 1225–1226
The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 4527, p. 2481
statutes.summary: This statute mandates the segregation of public schools by race, explicitly stating that white children cannot attend schools for colored children, and colored children cannot attend schools for white children. It also establishes a separate normal school for colored persons and outlines its governance. Teachers' institutes are to be organized separately for colored school officers and teachers.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 4762
statutes.title: § 4762. Judgment—minor to be apprenticed—duty of clerk.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 4762, p. 1674
statutes.summary: This statute outlines the legal process for identifying, trying, and punishing individuals deemed vagrants. Convicted vagrants over twenty-one years of age could be bound out to labor or sold into servitude for up to twelve months. Minors would be apprenticed until the age of twenty-one. The proceeds from the sale of a vagrant were to be used first for prosecution fees, then to pay the vagrant's debts, and any remainder was to be paid to the wife and children, or the vagrant upon completion of their term. Married men with families could be discharged if they posted bond to support their families and engage in honest work. The statute also details the rights and powers of those who purchased or took in a vagrant.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 796
statutes.title: § 796. No discrimination in coaches or compartments.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 796, p. 446
The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 3, 1918, § 796, p. 293
The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 796, p. 597
The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 796, pp. 597–598
The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 796, pp. 699–700
statutes.summary: This statute requires railroad companies operating in Kentucky to provide separate coaches or compartments for white and colored passengers. Each compartment must be divided by a substantial wooden partition with a door and clearly marked with appropriate words indicating the race for which it is designated. The law also stipulates that there should be no discrimination in the quality, convenience, or accommodations provided for either race. Failure to comply results in a misdemeanor charge and a fine for the railroad company. The statute also includes case law interpretations regarding company liability and the constitutionality of the separate coach law.

statutes.statute_citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 8, p. 72
statutes.title: § 8. In all elections for Representatives, every free male citizen (negroes, mulattoes, and Indians excepted), who at the time being, hath attained to the age of twenty -one years, and resided in the State two years, or the county or town in which he offers to vote one year next preceding the…
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Third Edition, 1903, § 8, p. 72
The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 1, 1915, § 8, p. 56
statutes.summary: This section of the Kentucky Constitution outlines the qualifications for electors in elections for Representatives. It explicitly excludes 'negroes, mulattoes, and Indians' from the right to vote, while granting suffrage to free male citizens who meet age and residency requirements. It also details the process for representation in the House and Senate.

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 120, pp. 311–312
statutes.title: AN ACT for the benefit of the Agricultural and Mechanical College of Kentucky, and appropriating money to pay existing deficiencies, and to provide additional income therefor.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 120, pp. 311–312
statutes.summary: This act appropriates $15,000 annually to the Agricultural and Mechanical College of Kentucky. It acknowledges that the college's income from federal land grants and appropriations is reduced by 14% because it must be shared with a "colored normal school" for the maintenance of the Black population. The act also addresses a deficit accumulated by the college due to increased expenditures.

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 31, p. 108
statutes.title: AN ACT to amend section 1 of an act, entitled "An Act to authorize trustees of county seminary and school property, owned or held in trust by trustees by a majority of their board, to dispose of same to trustees of common school districts embracing same," approved March 17, 1896.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 31, p. 108
statutes.summary: This act amends a previous law to allow trustees of county seminaries, established before December 18, 1865, to sell or dispose of seminary property to trustees of white common school districts. The property or its proceeds must be used for the education of white pupils in those districts, with provisions for white pupils from other districts to receive a reduction to compensate for their interest in the seminary property.

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 36, pp. 132–134
statutes.title: AN ACT to provide for the establishing of graded schools in common school districts bordering on county lines.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 36, pp. 132–134
statutes.summary: This act allows for the establishment of graded common school districts by petitioning county judges. It specifies that the election to approve the establishment and taxation for such schools must be held for 'legal white voters' and that taxes can be levied on property belonging to 'said white voters or corporations' or as a poll tax on 'each white male inhabitant over twenty-one years of age'.

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 51, pp. 148–150
statutes.title: AN ACT creating the thirty-first judicial district of Kentucky, fixing the time of holding courts thereof, providing for the election of a circuit judge and Commonwealth's attorney, and changing the twenty -third and twenty -fourth districts of Kentucky so as to provide for said thirty-first…
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 51, pp. 148–150
statutes.summary: This act creates a new judicial district (thirty-first) and adjusts existing ones (twenty-third and twenty-fourth) due to population growth and resource development. It also includes a provision for paying patrols, with higher pay in counties over 150,000 inhabitants. The patrol payment is set at a maximum of one dollar per ten hours of duty, or two dollars in larger counties at the court's discretion. Patrols must present claims for services, specifying hours and verified by oath.

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 53, pp. 152–154
statutes.title: AN ACT to empower cities of the fourth class to separate the management and control of their schools where the same are now under the control of a board of education.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 53, pp. 152–154
statutes.summary: This act allows cities of the fourth class in Kentucky to separate their existing graded free schools into distinct white and colored common schools, managed and controlled by a Board of Education. This separation can be enacted by ordinance.

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 6, pp. 54–56
statutes.title: AN ACT to amend an act, entitled An act to regulate elections in this Commonwealth, approved June 30, 1892.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 6, pp. 54–56
statutes.summary: This act amends a previous election law by expanding the requirement for voter registration to include cities and towns of the fifth and sixth classes. It also mandates that election officers issue a certificate of registration to each voter, and that no person may vote without presenting this certificate.

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 85, pp. 204–205
statutes.title: AN ACT to prohibit white and colored persons from attending the same school.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1904, ch. 85, pp. 204–205
statutes.summary: This act makes it illegal for any person, corporation, or association to operate a college, school, or institution that admits both white and negro races as pupils. Violators face a fine of one thousand dollars, and an additional one hundred dollars for each day the school is operated after conviction. Instructors teaching in such institutions are also subject to the same fines.

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 118, pp. 454–457
statutes.title: AN ACT to amend section four thousand three hundred and fifteen, Kentucky Statutes.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 118, pp. 454–457
statutes.summary: This statute outlines the responsibilities of supervisors in overseeing road work performed by delinquent taxpayers and convicts, including the use of chains to prevent escape. It establishes a system where delinquent taxpayers can work off their fines through labor on roads, which historically has been applied in a racially discriminatory manner.

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 156, pp. 542–555
statutes.title: AN ACT to amend sections two thousand two hundred and forty-one, two thousand two hundred and forty-two, and two thousand two hundred and forty-three, and repealing and providing a substitute for section two thousand two hundred and forty -seven of the Kentucky Statutes, compiled and edited by John…
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 156, pp. 542–555
statutes.summary: This statute amends existing laws regarding jury selection in Kentucky, including provisions for separate jury wheels in counties with circuit courts of continuous sessions, which may imply racial segregation in jury selection processes.

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 18, pp. 83–100
statutes.title: AN ACT creating and establishing a Board of Commissioners, to be known as the Kentucky State Board of Control for Charitable Institutions, and prescribing its duties and powers.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 18, pp. 83–100
statutes.summary: This statute outlines the procedures for the reception and care of patients in asylums, explicitly stating that white and colored patients shall not be kept in the same building, indicating a racial segregation policy.

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 22, pp. 111–271
statutes.title: AN ACT relating to Revenue and Taxation.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 22, pp. 111–271
statutes.summary: This statute outlines the taxation of railroad and bridge companies in school districts, specifying that the funds collected from white and colored school districts are to be distributed based on the number of white and colored children, thereby reinforcing racial segregation in educational funding.

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 51, pp. 316–319
statutes.title: AN ACT to repeal chapter two hundred and ninety -six of the Session Acts of eighteen hundred and eighty-seven and eighteen hundred and eignty-eight.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 51, pp. 316–319
statutes.summary: This statute establishes the Albany High School as a corporation and outlines its governance, specifically stating that it will receive funding for white children only, thereby enforcing racial segregation in education.

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 55, pp. 326–328
statutes.title: AN ACT relating to amendment of section one hundred and forty—five of the Constitution, relating to suffrage and elections.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 55, pp. 326–328
statutes.summary: This statute amends the Kentucky Constitution to require that individuals must have paid all state, county, municipal, district, and school taxes at least sixty days before an election in order to be eligible to vote. This provision effectively disenfranchises those who cannot afford to pay these taxes, which disproportionately affects Black citizens and other marginalized groups.

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 56, pp. 328–329
statutes.title: AN ACT appropriating money for industrial training for colored persons and for completing girls' dormitory and providing water for ordinary use and fire protection at Kentucky Normal Industrial Institute.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 56, pp. 328–329
statutes.summary: This statute appropriates funds for the Kentucky Normal and Industrial Institute for colored persons, addressing the need for industrial training and improvements to facilities specifically for Black youth.

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 57, pp. 329–335
statutes.title: AN ACT to amend an act, entitled "An act for the government of cities of the first class," approved July first, eighteen hundred and ninety—three.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 57, pp. 329–335
statutes.summary: This statute includes provisions for the training of colored youth in industrious habits and useful trades, indicating a segregated approach to education and vocational training.

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 59, p. 338
statutes.title: AN ACT to make it unlawful to present plays in this Commonwealth that are based upon antagonism alleged formerly to exist between master and slave or that excite race prejudice, and to provide a penalty therefor.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1906, ch. 59, p. 338
statutes.summary: This statute makes it unlawful to present plays that are based on the historical antagonism between master and slave or that excite race prejudice, imposing fines and imprisonment for violations.

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1908, ch. 56, pp. 150–160
statutes.title: AN ACT for the government and regulation of the Common Schools of the State.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1908, ch. 56, pp. 150–160
statutes.summary: This act establishes that each county will compose one school district, with an exception for cities or towns that maintain a separate system of public schools. The remaining part of the county outside such a city or town district will constitute a school district. Within thirty days of the act taking effect, county officials will divide each county school district into educational divisions with an equal number of school-aged children, including both white and colored children, based on the last census.

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1908, ch. 62, pp. 174–180
statutes.title: AN ACT to amend an act approved March the 21st, 1906, entitled, " An Act to establish a system of State Normal Schools in Kentucky; to create a Board of Regents for the general management thereof; to create a Normal Exec nti ve Council, which shall determine the requirements for admission and…
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1908, ch. 62, pp. 174–180
statutes.summary: This act amends a previous law establishing State Normal Schools in Kentucky. It divides the state into two districts, Eastern and Western, for the Eastern Kentucky State Normal School (Richmond) and the Western Kentucky State Normal School (Bowling Green). The boundaries of these districts are to be determined by a commission based on white population, aiming for districts that are as equal as possible in white population.

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1908, ch. 64, pp. 186–187
statutes.title: AN ACT for additional improvements at the Kentucky Normal and Industrial Institute for Colored Persons.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1908, ch. 64, pp. 186–187
statutes.summary: This act appropriates $40,000 for the Kentucky Normal and Industrial Institute for Colored Persons in Frankfort, Kentucky. The funds are designated for paying outstanding debts from land purchases, and for the erection and equipment of an auditorium, practice school, and mechanical shop.

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1908, ch. 71, pp. 225–227
statutes.title: AN ACT to amend section 4375 of the Kentucky Statutes, Carroll's Edition, 1903.
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1908, ch. 71, pp. 225–227
statutes.summary: This act amends a previous law concerning burial associations. The provided text also discusses the apportionment of surplus funds in the State Treasury for white and colored schools, with interest accruing at six percent per annum. It specifies that the per capita derived from this interest shall be apportioned to white and colored schools respectively. The act also addresses the equitable apportionment of surplus funds when new counties are formed from existing ones that have such a surplus.

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1908, p. 24
statutes.title: Amendment to statute regarding student appointments to the Agricultural and Mechanical College
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1908, p. 24
statutes.summary: This statute amends a previous law to specify that each county in Kentucky is entitled to appoint one white pupil annually to the Agricultural and Mechanical College for every three thousand white school children, and one for each fraction thereof over fifteen hundred, based on the last official census. Each county is guaranteed at least one appointment. The appointed students receive free tuition, matriculation fees, room rent, fuel, and lights, along with other university advantages, except for board.

statutes.statute_citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, p. 301
statutes.title: General Provisions for Charitable Institutions (Asylums)
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, p. 301
statutes.summary: This statute outlines general provisions for charitable institutions, specifically asylums. It mandates that white and colored patients shall not be kept in the same building. It also details procedures for admitting and discharging patients, including provisions for pauper idiots, pay patients from other states, and criminal patients. The Board of Control is directed to ensure asylums are kept full and receive their due proportion of patients, while also enforcing racial segregation within the facilities.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 1376c
statutes.title: § 1376c. 1. Plays that excite race prejudice forbidden—penalty.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 1376c, p. 697
statutes.summary: This statute makes it unlawful for any person to present, or participate in the presentation of, any play that is based upon antagonism alleged to exist between master and slave, or that excites race prejudice. Violators are subject to a fine or imprisonment, or both.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 1399a
statutes.title: § 1399a. Slave marriages—children to inherit—children of subsequent marriage.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 1399a, p. 703
The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 1399a, pp. 703–704
Supplement to 1909 Kentucky Statutes, 1915, § 1399a, pp. 339–342
statutes.summary: This statute addresses the legitimacy and inheritance rights of children born from slave marriages. It states that children born from cohabitation between enslaved individuals as husband and wife are considered lawful children and legal heirs. However, if either parent later legally marries another person and has children from that subsequent marriage, the children from the slave marriage will only inherit a proportion of the property based on the ratio of children from the slave marriage to children from the subsequent legal marriage. The act also specifies that it does not apply if the property has already been sold to innocent purchasers or divided.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 1477a
statutes.title: § 1477a. Printed oaths—voter may be required to swear—penalties against voter and election officer.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 1477a, pp. 735–736
Kentucky election laws, primary law and Corrupt Practice Act, 1919, § 1477a, pp. 31–33
statutes.summary: This statute outlines the process for challenging a voter's qualifications and requires voters to take a detailed oath affirming their age, residency, and lack of felony convictions. It specifies the number of witnesses allowed in a dispute and mandates that the oath be subscribed and sworn before an election judge. The subscribed oath is to be returned to the county clerk and then to the grand jury, with penalties for failure to do so. The oath itself includes specific residency requirements and a declaration of no disqualification.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 2971
statutes.title: § 2971. Es cheated property—concerning.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 2971, pp. 1296–1299
statutes.summary: This statute mandates the separate maintenance and keeping of schools for white and colored children, prohibiting white children from attending schools for colored children and vice versa.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 3588a
statutes.title: § 3588a. Graded white and colored schools provision for.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 3588a, pp. 1513–1514
The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 2, 1915, § 3588a, pp. 428–429
The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 3588a, p. 2027
statutes.summary: This statute allows cities of the fourth class that have already established a system of free graded schools to separate them into distinct white and colored common schools. It mandates that taxes raised from white individuals or corporations cannot be used for colored schools, and vice versa. Each system will be governed by a board of six trustees and supported by a pro rata share of the State School Fund and local taxation.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 3780
statutes.title: § 3780.County court to appoint jurisdiction of patrols.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 3780, p. 1598
statutes.summary: This statute outlines the appointment, duties, and compensation of patrols in Kentucky counties. County courts are authorized to divide counties into districts and appoint patrols to maintain public peace and order. Patrols are tasked with visiting suspected places and places of unlawful assemblies. Compensation is based on hours of service, with a higher rate for counties with over 150,000 inhabitants. A separate section addresses the appointment of patrolmen in counties with first-class cities, with compensation paid by petitioners or employers.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 4372
statutes.title: § 4372.School fund can not be ap pro pri-ated or devoted to the payment of teachers not acting under the control or supervision of the officers of the common schools.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4372, pp. 1814–1815
statutes.summary: This statute details the distribution and management of the common school fund in Kentucky. It outlines the process for estimating and apportioning funds based on pupil-child census data, the role of the Auditor and Superintendent of Public Instruction, and procedures for handling uncalled-for or unused funds. Crucially, it states that the per capita derived from interest on bonded surplus in the State Treasury shall be duly apportioned to the white and colored schools of the county respectively.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 4426a
statutes.title: § 4426a. (1) County to compose school district—exceptions.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4426a, pp. 1840–1847
The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 2, 1915, § 4426a, p. 843
The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 2, 1915, § 4426a, pp. 843–850

The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 4426a, pp. 2256–2257
The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 4426a, pp. 2428–2429
statutes.summary: This statute outlines the process for dividing school districts into educational divisions and sub-districts. It explicitly mentions the inclusion of both white and colored children in these divisions and sub-districts. However, it also contains provisions that disproportionately affect Black students, such as the requirement that sub-districts must have at least fifty white children of school age to receive per capita funding for one teacher, and no more than one hundred white pupil-children for the payment of one teacher. This implies a potential underfunding or lack of resources for schools with a higher proportion of Black students.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 4427
statutes.title: § 4427.(1)Boundary.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4427, p. 1847
statutes.summary: This statute outlines the organization and administration of common school districts in Kentucky. It details rules for district boundaries, pupil population requirements, and the establishment of schools. Crucially, it contains a clause stating that 'nothing in this chapter shall be construed to authorize any white person to attend a common school or other institution of learning established for colored children.'

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 4439a
statutes.title: § 4439a. Seminary property may be acquired by trustees.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4439a, p. 1854
The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 3, 1918, § 4439a, pp. 1171–1172
The Kentucky Statutes, Sixth Edition, 1922, § 4439a, p. 2441
statutes.summary: This statute authorizes trustees holding legal title to county seminary property (acquired before December 18, 1865) to sell, transfer, or convey it to the trustees of white common school districts where the seminary property is located. The proceeds or property must be used for the education of white pupils, with provisions for white pupils from other districts to receive a reduction to compensate for their interest in the seminary property.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 4441
statutes.title: § 4441. Additional tax may be levied to pay indebtedness.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4441, p. 1856
statutes.summary: This statute, § 4442, states that a tax levied to pay indebtedness for schoolhouses shall be collected as provided by law for the present school tax. However, it includes a proviso that 'no tax shall be levied or collected from the property of colored persons to pay any indebtedness incurred for the benefit of schools for white children.'

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 4464a
statutes.title: § 4464a.Graded schools for two counties near line, how established.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4464a, pp. 1868–1869
statutes.summary: This statute outlines the process for establishing graded common schools that could span two counties. It specifies that the establishment of such a school and the levying of taxes for its maintenance and construction require a vote of the 'legal white voters' within the proposed district. The statute also details requirements for petitions, approvals from county judges and superintendents, and the proximity of the schoolhouse to the district's boundary.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 4526a
statutes.title: § 4526a. (1) White and colored not to be taught in same college—penalty.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4526a, p. 1893
Supplement to 1909 Kentucky Statutes, 1915, § 4526a, pp. 1186–1190
The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 2, 1915, § 4526a, p. 904
Common School Laws of Kentucky, 1916, § 210, pp. 110–111

statutes.summary: This statute mandates the separation of white and colored individuals in educational institutions. It prohibits teaching both races in the same college, school, or institution, with penalties for violations. It also makes it unlawful for individuals of one race to attend schools where the other race is received as pupils, with fines for each day of attendance. Exceptions are made for penal institutions and houses of reform. The law also allows for separate and distinct branches of private institutions in different localities, at least twenty-five miles apart, for the exclusive education of one race.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 4529
statutes.title: § 4529. Trustees—powers concerning studies—instructors and teachers.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4529, pp. 1894–1895
The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 2, 1915, § 4529, pp. 905–906
statutes.summary: This statute establishes and appropriates funds for a normal school specifically for colored residents of Kentucky. It outlines admission requirements, including age, health, moral character, and a pledge to teach in colored common schools. Tuition is free for eligible colored residents. The statute also forbids sectarian teaching but promotes Christian morality. It details trustee responsibilities for school inspection and reporting, and specifies annual appropriations for teacher salaries and expenses, as well as a separate appropriation for a dormitory for female pupils. Additional appropriations for buildings and support are noted from earlier acts.

statutes.title: § 4535a. (1) Two normal school districts—style of.

statutes.summary: This statute establishes two State Normal School districts, Eastern and Western Kentucky, with the Eastern located in Richmond and the Western in Bowling Green. It outlines the object of these schools as providing training for teachers to make common schools efficient. Notably, it states that diplomas from the normal department will entitle teachers to teach in any of the 'colored common schools' of the state. The districts are to be divided based on white population.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 4591a
statutes.title: § 4591a. Bond for benefit of Agricultural and Mechanical College and Colored Normal School—payment of interest.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4591a, pp. 1917–1918
statutes.summary: This statute details the allocation of interest from a perpetual bond of the Commonwealth of Kentucky to two educational institutions: the Agricultural and Mechanical College of Kentucky and the State Normal School for Colored Persons of Kentucky. The total annual interest of $4,950 is divided, with $627.75 allocated to the State Normal School for Colored Persons and $4,322.25 to the Agricultural and Mechanical College. This section is derived from an act of May 21, 1897, which also included initial appropriations to these institutions.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 4600
statutes.title: § 4600. Auditor and Treasurer - duties relating to.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4600, pp. 1919–1920
statutes.summary: This statute details the allocation of interest from a state bond to two educational institutions: the Agricultural and Mechanical College of Kentucky and the State Normal School for Colored Persons of Kentucky. It specifies the proportion of interest each institution receives, with the State Normal School for Colored Persons receiving $627.75 and the Agricultural and Mechanical College receiving $4,322.25 annually from a total interest payment of $4,950. The statute also references a prior appropriation act for both institutions.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 4636a
statutes.title: § 4636a. (1) State University established.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fourth Edition, 1909, § 4636a, pp. 1931–1934
The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 2, 1915, § 4636a, pp. 952–955
statutes.summary: This statute amends the law regarding student appointments to the State University (Agricultural and Mechanical College). It specifies that each county is entitled to appoint one white pupil for every three thousand white schoolchildren, and one for each fraction thereof over fifteen hundred, based on the last official census. Each county is guaranteed at least one annual appointment. The statute also outlines the selection process through competitive examinations open to individuals between fourteen and twenty-four years old, with preference given to those who have passed through public schools, possess energy and industry, and have limited means. The selection is made by county superintendents. Additionally, it mentions free tuition for students of the ministry at the university's discretion.

statutes.statute_citation: The Common School Laws of Kentucky, 1910, p. 184
statutes.title: School Taxation
citations: The Common School Laws of Kentucky, 1910, p. 184
statutes.summary: This section of the Common School Laws from 1910 details the apportionment of railroad taxes between white and colored schools within the same district. It specifies that stock owned by colored persons is liable for colored schools, and stock owned by white persons is liable for white schools. Agreements between trustees for different apportionment methods are deemed nullities.

statutes.statute_citation: The Common School Laws of Kentucky, 1910, p. 185
statutes.title: Tax Exemption for Graded Schools
citations: The Common School Laws of Kentucky, 1910, p. 185
statutes.summary: An act providing a tax on property owned by white persons for the maintenance of graded schools for white pupils implicitly exempts the property of black persons from this tax. A corporation seeking tax exemption must prove its owners are black.

statutes.statute_citation: The Common School Laws of Kentucky, 1910, p. 187
statutes.title: Common School Laws 1910
citations: The Common School Laws of Kentucky, 1910, p. 187
statutes.summary: This excerpt from the 1910 Common School Laws of Kentucky addresses various aspects of school district organization, taxation, and student eligibility. Notably, it states that taxes raised under a special act for the benefit of a district school for whites must be distributed pro rata between white and colored schools under general law. This indicates a legally mandated separation or differential treatment based on race within the education system.

It mandates that county superintendents, judges, and attorneys divide each county school district into educational divisions based on an equal number of school-aged children, explicitly mentioning 'white and colored children'.

The duties of this visitor are stated to be identical to those of the subdistrict trustee concerning the colored school(s).

This explicitly acknowledges and implies separate, potentially unequal, funding or resource allocation based on race.

It specifies that elections for approving taxes to fund these schools must be held for the 'legal white voters' within the proposed district. The statute also details requirements for petition approval by trustees and county superintendents, as well as geographical limitations for the school site.

It specifies that only legal white voters can vote on propositions to establish these districts and levy taxes for their maintenance and building. The process involves petitions, court orders, and elections, all explicitly limited to the 'legal white voters' and 'white male inhabitant'.

The Board of Education has the power to establish kindergartens, high schools, manual training schools, and normal schools, and to prescribe rules for their government and employ teachers.

The selection process involves the County Superintendent examining applicants and choosing those with the highest qualifications and good character. citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1912, ch. 130, pp. 493–496

statutes.summary: This statute empowers the Board of Education to establish and maintain separate schools for colored children, indicating a legal framework for racial segregation in education.

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1912, ch. 145, pp. 678–679

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1912, ch. 25, pp. 144–157

statutes.summary: This statute outlines the creation of educational divisions for schoolchildren in Kentucky, explicitly mentioning the inclusion of both white and colored children while establishing boundaries that favor existing school districts for white children.

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1912, ch. 64, pp. 241–242

citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1912, ch. 64, pp. 241–242
statutes.summary: This statute repeals a previous act that established a common school specifically for the benefit of colored people in Catlettsburg and vicinity, indicating a discriminatory approach to education.

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1912, ch. 98, pp. 306–307

citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1912, ch. 98, pp. 306–307
statutes.summary: This statute increases the per capita allowance for white deaf pupils at the Kentucky School for the Deaf and extends the same allowance to colored deaf pupils, reflecting a segregated educational system.

citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1914, ch. 61, pp. 181–183
statutes.summary: This statute mandates the provision of separate apartments for children of white and colored races committed to the Houses of Reform, reflecting the segregationist policies characteristic of Jim Crow laws.

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1914, ch. 64, pp. 191–198
statutes.title: AN ACT to amend Sections 4464, 4464a, 4480, 4482, Article 10, Kentucky Statutes, Carroll's Edition, 1909, and repealing Section 4464b thereof, and amending said Article 10, of said Statutes, relating to schools, by adding thereto Section 4500b.

statutes.summary: This statute outlines the process for establishing graded common school districts in Kentucky, allowing for the creation of high schools and the payment of tuition for eligible students. It specifies that only legal white voters can participate in the decision-making process regarding these schools.

statutes.summary: This statute outlines the requirements for individuals seeking to be licensed as chauffeurs in Kentucky, including the need to disclose their color and provide a character certificate, which may imply racial discrimination in the licensing process.

citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1914, ch. 74, pp. 292–296
statutes.summary: This statute outlines the requirements for issuing marriage licenses in Kentucky, including the collection of racial information, which indicates a legal distinction based on race.

citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1914, ch. 84, pp. 457–466
statutes.summary: This statute mandates that the state board of examiners prepare separate series of examination questions for white and colored teachers, indicating a clear racial distinction in the educational certification process.

statutes.statute_citation: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1914, p. 441
statutes.title: Amendment to Ballot Provision for Women Voters
citations: Acts of the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, 1914, p. 441
statutes.summary: This statute amends the provisions regarding the number of official ballots to be provided for elections, specifically ensuring that women voters receive a number of ballots equal to fifty percent of those provided for male voters, thereby institutionalizing a differential treatment based on gender, which can be seen as part of the broader Jim Crow laws that enforced segregation and discrimination.

statutes.statute_citation: Kentucky Common School Laws, 1914, p. 197
statutes.title: Rulings of the Department
citations: Kentucky Common School Laws, 1914, p. 197
statutes.summary: This section contains various rulings related to the administration of common schools in Kentucky. Notably, it states that taxes raised under a special act for the benefit of a district school for whites must be distributed pro rata between white and colored schools under general law. Other rulings cover the powers and responsibilities of county superintendents, boards of education, and school trustees, as well as issues related to taxation and elections for school districts.

statutes.statute_citation: Kentucky Common School Laws, 1914, p. 199
statutes.title: Common Schools - School fund application and eligibility
citations: Kentucky Common School Laws, 1914, p. 199
statutes.summary: This ruling clarifies that the school fund can only be applied to schools that are legally established, taught by qualified teachers, and open to all white children within a specified age range in the district. It also states that no appropriation for normal schools can be constitutionally made from the school fund.

statutes.statute_citation: Kentucky Common School Laws, 1914, p. 201
statutes.title: School Taxation - Apportionment of Railroad Tax
citations: Kentucky Common School Laws, 1914, p. 201
statutes.summary: This section of the Kentucky Common School Laws from 1914 addresses the apportionment of railroad taxes for school purposes. It states that railroad taxes shall be divided between white and colored schools within the same district. However, this provision does not apply to taxes on property of other corporations. For private corporations, stock owned by colored persons is only liable for colored schools, and stock owned by white persons is only liable for white schools. Any agreement between white and colored school trustees to apportion taxes differently than required by law is considered null and void.

statutes.statute_citation: Kentucky Common School Laws, 1914, § 443, p. 170
statutes.title: § 443. Free Tuition to Certain Students.
citations: Kentucky Common School Laws, 1914, § 443, p. 170
statutes.summary: This statute outlines the provisions for free tuition and other benefits at the Agricultural and Mechanical College (later the University of Kentucky). It specifies that counties are entitled to send a certain number of "white pupils" based on the white school child population. It also mentions that the Board of Trustees may grant free tuition to students preparing for the ministry in connection with any "white religious denomination."

statutes.statute_citation: Kentucky Common School Laws, 1914, § 514, pp. 190–191
statutes.title: § 514. $ 15,000 Appropriated for Dormitory -The sum of fifteen thousand dollars is hereby appropriated for the purpose of building a dormitory for the use of the female pupils of the State Normal School for Colored Persons, to be paid by the Auditor of Public Accounts out of any money in the…
citations: Kentucky Common School Laws, 1914, § 514, pp. 190–191
statutes.summary: This section of the Kentucky Common School Laws from 1914 details the funding, reporting, and certification processes for the Colored Normal School. It outlines an annual appropriation of $3,000 for teachers and expenses, the establishment of a 'Colored Normal School Fund,' and the authorization for the Board to grant certificates of proficiency and diplomas to graduates, entitling them to teach in 'colored common schools.' It also notes a name change to 'The Kentucky Normal and Industrial Institute for Colored Persons' and an appropriation for a dormitory for female pupils.

It also includes general rulings on graded common school districts and teacher certification.

Crucially, it mandates that the State Board of Examiners prepare separate series of examination questions for white teachers and colored teachers, all of the same grade. This establishes a system of racial segregation in the certification process for teachers in common schools.

statutes.statute_citation: Kentucky Laws Made Plain, 1914, p. 64
statutes.title: HUSBAND AND WIFE
citations: Kentucky Laws Made Plain, 1914, p. 64
statutes.summary: This statute outlines marriage requirements in Kentucky, including the need for a license, parental consent for minors, and specifies that it is unlawful for a white person to marry a negro. It also details conditions under which marriage is void, such as idiocy, lunacy, existing marriage without divorce, or if the male is under 14 and the female under 12. The statute also touches upon property rights of married women and inheritance rights of surviving spouses.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 185
statutes.title: SEC. 185. (1) The provision of Ky.
citations: Supplement to 1909 Kentucky Statutes, 1915, § 185, p. 1313
statutes.summary: This section of annotations to the Kentucky Constitution, specifically referencing Section 187, includes a case (Crosby v. City of Mayfield) that discusses the submission of propositions to incur indebtedness to furnish a white school with buildings and the maintenance of white schools by taxable property owned by white persons. It also includes a case (Mullins v. Belcher) that defines a child with an appreciable mixture of negro blood as a colored child. These annotations directly address racial segregation in education.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 2089c
statutes.title: SEC. 2089c. Columbus Day made legal holiday.
citations: Supplement to 1909 Kentucky Statutes, 1915, § 2089c, pp. 489–490
statutes.summary: This statute mandates that children committed to the Houses of Reform must be provided with separate apartments based on their race (white and colored).

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 2978b
statutes.title: SEC. 2978b. 24.
citations: Supplement to 1909 Kentucky Statutes, 1915, § 2978b, pp. 812–814
statutes.summary: This statute mandates that school boards in first-class municipalities must provide, maintain, and support separate schools for all bona fide resident colored children between the ages of six and twenty years. These schools are to be operated in a similar manner to those for white children and are entitled to the same benefits, rules, regulations, and restrictions.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 298d
statutes.title: SEC. 298d. APPROPRIATION IN 1910.
citations: Supplement to 1909 Kentucky Statutes, 1915, § 298d, pp. 66–67
The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 1, 1915, § 298d, p. 321
statutes.summary: This statute clarifies the operational and financial separation of schools for white and colored deaf students. It mandates that these schools be maintained as distinct institutions, though under a single Board of Commissioners and superintendent. Crucially, it specifies that the school for white deaf students is entitled to all appropriations unless explicitly designated for the colored deaf school, while the colored deaf school is only entitled to appropriations where the term 'colored' is used to distinguish it. Funds for each school must be kept separate and expended accordingly.

statutes.summary: This act amends the per capita allowance for white deaf pupils in the Kentucky School for the Deaf, increasing it from $140 to $150 per annum. Crucially, it explicitly states that the same per capita allowance made to white deaf pupils shall also apply to pupils of the school for the colored deaf. It also details the payment of appropriations and declares an emergency for the act to take effect.

statutes.title: SEC. 3212-11. 38.
citations: Supplement to 1909 Kentucky Statutes, 1915, § 3212-11, pp. 899–901
statutes.summary: This statute outlines the educational provisions for municipalities of the second class in Kentucky. It explicitly states that 'colored children' may be taught in a manner similar to white children and that these colored schools are entitled to the same benefits, rules, regulations, and restrictions as white schools. It also details the powers and duties of the Board of Education regarding admissions, textbooks, religious instruction, and reporting to the State Superintendent.

It also grants the Board the power to establish kindergartens, high schools, night schools, and normal training classes, and to prescribe rules and regulations for their operation.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 4398g

statutes.summary: This statute outlines the requirements for County Superintendents in Kentucky, including bonding, salary, office provision, and election procedures. Specifically, it details that in counties with cities of the first or second class that maintain separate school systems, the County Superintendent must reside outside these cities and be elected by voters residing outside these cities. It also specifies the salary, payment, and office requirements for the County Superintendent, with exceptions for counties with low taxable property.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 4425f

It also addresses various administrative and financial aspects of school districts, including the recovery of bond violations, the effect of prior judgments, women's voting rights in school elections, poll taxes for school purposes, fiscal court compliance with education board estimates, the handling of tax collections for sheriff compensation, the process for electing teachers when the county superintendent is absent, the eligibility of teachers with valid certificates, the entitlement of colored common school districts to railroad taxes, the location and funding of high schools, and the powers of the County School Superintendent versus the County Board of Education.

It specifies that only legal white voters can vote on the proposition to establish such a district and to approve annual taxes for its maintenance and building needs. The statute also details requirements for district boundaries, the number of pupils, and the approval process by county education officials.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 4481a

It specifies that the tax can only be levied on property owned by white persons, companies, or corporations, and the poll tax can only be levied on white male citizens over twenty-one years of age residing within the district. It also details provisions for bond payments and sinking funds.

It mandates separate but identically managed institutions under a single board of commissioners and superintendent. Funding for the white deaf school is to be derived from general appropriations unless specifically designated for the colored deaf school, which is only entitled to funds explicitly mentioning 'colored'.

statutes.statute_citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 2, 1915, p. 101
statutes.title: Separate schools for white and colored children.
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 2, 1915, p. 101
statutes.summary: This statute mandates the establishment and maintenance of separate schools for white and colored children within first-class cities. It stipulates that colored children, aged six to twenty, who are bona fide residents, will be taught in a similar manner to white children. These separate schools for colored children are entitled to the same benefits, governed by the same rules and regulations, and subject to the same restrictions as schools for white children.

statutes.title: Municipal Corporations - Public Schools
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 2, 1915, p. 292
statutes.summary: This statute outlines the powers and responsibilities of the board of education in second-class cities, specifically addressing the establishment and maintenance of public schools. Crucially, it mandates the provision of separate schools for colored children, ensuring they receive the same benefits and are governed by the same rules as schools for white children. The statute also covers kindergarten, high schools, night schools, normal training classes, textbook provision, and religious instruction.

statutes.statute_citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 2, 1915, p. 852
statutes.title: SCHOOLS - COMMON . Districts - Trustees - Teachers - Taxation .
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 2, 1915, p. 852
statutes.summary: This statute outlines the organization and administration of common schools in Kentucky. It details the powers and duties of county boards of education, including employing teachers, fixing salaries, prescribing courses of study, and selecting textbooks. It also addresses the consolidation of school subdistricts, specifying that consolidation should consider the needs of "white or colored children." Furthermore, it prohibits school officials from having financial interests in school contracts and establishes penalties for violations. The statute is an amendment to Chapter 113, Article VIa, Section 4426a of Carroll's Kentucky Statutes, 1909.

It specifies that such property or its proceeds must be used for the education of white pupils, with provisions for white pupils from other districts to receive a reduction in fees to compensate for their interest in the seminary property. The statute also outlines procedures for condemning schoolhouses, levying taxes for repairs and construction, and borrowing money for school facilities.

The selection process involves the county superintendent examining applicants and choosing those with the highest qualifications and good character. The statute also requires appointed pupils to declare their intent to teach in public schools for a specified period to receive free tuition.

It specifies the interest payments to be made semi-annually to each institution, with a clear distinction in the amounts allocated. The statute also outlines the general powers and duties of the commissioners of the sinking fund regarding the protection of the state's credit and management of public debt.

The boundaries of these divisions are to follow existing school districts for white children as closely as possible. The statute also allows for the subdivision of these divisions into school subdistricts, again following the boundaries of existing school districts for white children. Graded common school districts and school districts within municipal districts are exempt from these provisions.

statutes.statute_citation: The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary 2, 1916, p. 1136
statutes.title: Separate Coach Law Application to Sleeping Cars
citations: The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary 2, 1916, p. 1136
statutes.summary: This statute discusses the application of Kentucky's separate coach law (Ky. Stats., Sec. 795) to sleeping cars. It clarifies that a sleeping car owned and operated by a Pullman Car Company, even when attached to a defendant company's passenger train, is not considered 'operated' by the defendant company under the separate coach law. Therefore, the defendant company is not liable for hauling a sleeping car without separate compartments or for failing to ensure a colored passenger in such a sleeper entered the day coach compartment set aside for their race, especially when the passenger had purchased a ticket entitling them to ride in the sleeper.

statutes.statute_citation: The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary 2, 1916, p. 191
statutes.title: FREIGHT TRAIN
citations: The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary 2, 1916, p. 191
statutes.summary: This statute addresses the application of separate coach requirements for white and colored passengers on freight trains. It states that Kentucky Statutes, Section 795, requiring separate coaches for white and colored passengers, does not apply to passengers in a caboose car attached to a freight train. The case discussed involved a defendant who sold tickets to both white and colored passengers for a caboose car on a branch line, with no separate compartments or signs. The court ruled that the caboose car on a freight train, even if carrying passengers, was exempt from the separate compartment requirement.

statutes.statute_citation: The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary 2, 1916, p. 262
statutes.title: GRADED SCHOOL DISTRICT
citations: The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary 2, 1916, p. 262
statutes.summary: This entry discusses graded school districts in Kentucky. It explicitly states that 'colored graded schools did not exist' when certain statutes were enacted in 1906, implying that these statutes were originally intended for white common schools. However, it also asserts that the terms 'graded school district' and 'common school district' were intended to be synonymous and interchangeable, suggesting that the existing legal framework for graded schools could be applied to colored schools. This indicates a legal interpretation that allowed for the application of graded school structures to separate educational systems for Black students, even if not explicitly named in the original legislation.

statutes.statute_citation: The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary 2, 1916, p. 372
statutes.title: IDENTITY
citations: The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary 2, 1916, p. 372
statutes.summary: This entry discusses the legal concept of 'identity' in various contexts, including ticket purchasers and money identification. Crucially, it references a statute (Ky. Stat., 796) and court cases (L. & N. R. Co. v. Com.) that address 'substantial equality of accommodations' for white and colored passengers, stating that equality does not mean identity. This implies a legal framework for separate but supposedly equal facilities.

statutes.statute_citation: The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary 2, 1916, p. 618
statutes.title: KNOWINGLY
citations: The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary 2, 1916, p. 618
statutes.summary: This entry defines the legal term 'knowingly' and provides examples of its application in Kentucky case law. One example specifically addresses a railroad company's violation of a statute requiring signs to indicate the race for which compartments on interurban cars were designated. The court presumed the violation was knowing and willful if the signs were absent.

statutes.statute_citation: The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary 2, 1916, p. 686
statutes.title: Legitimacy of Children in Kentucky
citations: The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary 2, 1916, p. 686
statutes.summary: This statute addresses the legitimacy of children born from various marriage circumstances in Kentucky. It specifically states that the issue of a marriage between a white person and a negro or mulatto shall not be legitimate. It also outlines conditions under which children from void marriages, marriages contracted in good faith with a presumed-dead spouse, or customary marriages of negroes and mulattoes prior to February 14, 1866, would be considered legitimate. The statute also details provisions for legitimizing children through subsequent marriage and recognition by the father.

statutes.statute_citation: The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary 2, 1916, p. 935
statutes.title: MULATTO
citations: The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary 2, 1916, p. 935
statutes.summary: This entry defines a 'mulatto' in the context of statutes that do not specifically define the term. It cites a case (Gentry v. McMinnis) that held a mulatto to be a person with at least one-fourth African blood. This definition is relevant to understanding racial classifications used in historical statutes, which often underpinned Jim Crow laws.

statutes.statute_citation: The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary 2, 1916, p. 938
statutes.title: An Act entitled " an Act for the benefit of Belle Point,"
citations: The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary 2, 1916, p. 938
statutes.summary: This statute describes an unconstitutional act that levied a tax on white citizens of a town to fund an additional five months of school. While white children within the town could attend for free, children residing outside the town limits but within the district were also allowed to attend free for the initial five months, but would have to pay tuition thereafter. The court found this unconstitutional because it taxed the town to educate the entire district.

statutes.statute_citation: The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary 3, 1916, p. 1193
statutes.title: WHITE PERSON - Taxation for Graded School Purposes
citations: The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary 3, 1916, p. 1193
statutes.summary: This entry discusses the taxation of property for graded school purposes. It states that a corporation's property is taxable under a statute authorizing taxation of 'white persons' for such purposes, unless the corporation can prove its corporators and stockholders are Black. The intent is for the burden to fall on all property within the district except that of Black individuals.

statutes.statute_citation: The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary 3, 1916, p. 261
statutes.title: PROPERTY TAX 2720 PROPS
citations: The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary 3, 1916, p. 261
statutes.summary: This entry from The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary (1916) states that the right to teach white and negro children in a private school at the same time and place is not a property right, citing Berea College v. Com. This implies a legal framework that would prevent integrated education, a hallmark of Jim Crow laws.

statutes.statute_citation: The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary 3, 1916, p. 621
statutes.title: SEGREGATION
citations: The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary 3, 1916, p. 621
statutes.summary: This entry defines segregation in the context of Louisville's municipal segregation ordinance. It states that the ordinance was a valid exercise of police power, deemed reasonable and expedient for public welfare. The purpose was to prevent violence stemming from racial antipathies and to preserve racial solidarity. It also references a note on the validity of segregation statutes or ordinances prohibiting persons of different races or colors from living in the same locality.

statutes.statute_citation: The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary 3, 1916, p. 642
statutes.title: Separate Coach Law
citations: The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary 3, 1916, p. 642
statutes.summary: This statute, known as the "Separate Coach Law" (Ky. Stats., Secs. 795 and 796), mandates that railroad companies operating in Kentucky must provide separate coaches or cars for white and colored passengers. It specifies that compartments divided by a partition with a door will be considered separate coaches, and each must be clearly marked to indicate the race for which it is designated. The law also prohibits discrimination in the quality, convenience, or accommodations provided for white and colored passengers, stating that substantial equality, not identical accommodations, is required.

statutes.statute_citation: The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary 3, 1916, p. 643
statutes.title: The Separate Coach Law
citations: The Kentucky Judicial Dictionary 3, 1916, p. 643
statutes.summary: This entry discusses the constitutionality and application of Kentucky's Separate Coach Law, which mandated separate railway cars for white and colored passengers. It states that the law applies equally to both races and that colored passengers are entitled to the same redress as white passengers for violations. The entry also notes that the conductor, not the railroad company, is liable for failure to assign passengers to their designated coaches.

statutes.statute_citation: The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 3, 1918, § 1, p. 30
statutes.title: § 1. An ordinance of the city of Louisville requiring the use of separate blocks for residences, places of abode and places of assembly for white and colored people, respectively, was sustained as constitutional. Harris v. City of Louisville, 165 Ky. 559,
citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 3, 1918, § 1, p. 30
statutes.summary: This section of the Kentucky Constitution, referencing a Louisville city ordinance, addresses the constitutionality of requiring separate residential blocks for white and colored people. While the ordinance was initially sustained, it was later reversed by the U.S. Supreme Court. The text also touches upon the principle of equal, though not necessarily identical, privileges for white and colored persons.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 2095b-28

citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 3, 1918, § 2095b-28, p. 590
statutes.summary: This statute outlines the procedures for committing girls to houses of reform, including qualifications for entrance, the process of commitment, and the return of girls found to be epileptic, insane, or feeble-minded. It also details the employment of visiting agents to find suitable homes for girls released on trial and the recall of girls who do not conduct themselves properly or lack a suitable home. Crucially, it mandates the segregation of white and colored races within these institutions. The statute also addresses the financial responsibilities of counties for transporting and maintaining committed girls, as well as the payment of expenses and salaries for the institution from the State treasury.

statutes.statute_citation: Ky. Stat. § 272a-9

It mandates the complete separation of inmates according to color and sex in the new buildings, and as far as practicable, separation of epileptics from non-epileptics. The statute also details the compensation of the superintendent, the process for employing architects, purchasing materials, and the selection and size of the farm.

statutes.summary: This statute amends a previous act to ensure that the per capita allowance for pupils in the school for the colored deaf is the same as that provided for pupils in the school for the white deaf. It also addresses compulsory education for deaf children.

citations: The Kentucky Statutes, Fifth Edition, v. 3, 1918, § 2, p. 30

While the ordinance was initially sustained, it was later reversed by the U.S. Supreme Court. The text also touches upon the principle of equal, though not necessarily identical, privileges for white and colored persons.
